note: Question bank for the glossary page's Daily 5 and for review quizzes. Built from every quiz in course/m*.json (source: "lesson", ids <lessonId>-q<n>) plus original questions (source: "bank", ids qb-<module>-<nn>). difficulty is easy | medium | hard; lesson questions inherit it from the module level.

questions.q: A company has 2,000,000 shares outstanding and its stock last traded at $25. What is its market capitalization?
choices: It cannot be computed without the company's profit
questions.explain: Market cap is price times shares outstanding: $25 x 2,000,000 = $50,000,000. Profit is not part of the formula; the market's opinion of future profit is already inside the price.

questions.q: You buy 10 shares of a company on an exchange. Who receives your money?
choices: The company, which uses it to grow
The exchange, which holds it in trust
Another investor who sold their shares
Your broker, as a deposit
questions.explain: After the IPO, shares trade on the secondary market between investors. The company only receives money when it issues new shares.

questions.q: A $40 stock pays a dividend of $0.30 every quarter. What is its annual dividend yield?
questions.explain: Four quarterly payments of $0.30 total $1.20 per year. $1.20 / $40 = 0.03, or 3%.

questions.q: Why does the backtest page show a buy-and-hold return next to each strategy?
choices: Because buy and hold is always the best strategy
To give you a benchmark; a strategy that underperforms simply holding the stock has not added value
Because it is required by securities regulations
To estimate dividends, which the simulator otherwise ignores
questions.explain: A strategy has to beat the lazy alternative to be worth its effort and risk. Buy and hold is the yardstick, not a recommendation.

questions.q: Which statement about short selling is correct?
choices: Your maximum loss is the amount you sold the shares for
You profit if the price falls and your potential loss is unlimited if it rises
It is impossible in a paper-trading account
It pays you the dividend instead of the owner
questions.explain: Selling borrowed shares at $100 and buying back at $80 earns $20, but if the stock rises to $300 you owe $200 per share, and there is no ceiling. Short sellers also owe any dividends to the lender.

questions.q: What are the regular trading hours of the US stock market?
choices: 8:00 am to 5:00 pm Eastern
9:30 am to 4:00 pm Eastern, Monday to Friday
9:00 am to 4:30 pm Pacific
24 hours a day on weekdays
questions.explain: The regular session runs 9:30 am to 4:00 pm Eastern. Pre-market and after-hours sessions exist but have far less volume.

questions.q: A stock closes at $60.00. That evening the company announces a large recall and the next morning the first trade is at $52.00. What is this called?
choices: A spread
A gap
A dividend
A halt
questions.explain: A gap is a jump between one session's close and the next session's open with no trades in between. News released while the market is closed is the usual cause.

questions.q: Which of these is generally the most liquid period of the trading day for large US stocks?
choices: The pre-market session at 6 am
The hour after the open and the last half hour before the close
Lunchtime, when institutions are away
The after-hours session after an earnings release
questions.explain: The open and the close concentrate the most volume, which is why the opening and closing auctions exist. This is a widely observed tendency, not a guarantee for any single day.

questions.q: Why do companies usually release earnings reports just after 4:00 pm Eastern?
choices: Regulations require it
So the first reaction happens in the thin after-hours session and investors have overnight to digest the report before the regular session
Because exchanges are closed for maintenance until then
To avoid paying dividends that day
questions.explain: Releasing outside regular hours gives analysts and investors time to read the report. The after-hours reaction is real but can be partly reversed at the next open.

questions.q: How does the paper-trading engine in this app fill a market order when the market is closed?
choices: It rejects the order
It queues it for the opening auction with realistic slippage
It fills at the last known price immediately
It fills at the previous day's low
questions.explain: The simulator fills market orders immediately at the last known price with no slippage, which is more forgiving than a real broker. The backtest page lets you add slippage to make results more honest.

questions.q: A stock is quoted bid $42.10, ask $42.14. You place an order to buy immediately. About what price will you pay?
choices: The previous close
questions.explain: Buyers who want to trade immediately pay the ask, the lowest price a seller is offering. Sellers who want immediacy receive the bid.

questions.q: Stock A is quoted $250.00 / $250.04. Stock B is quoted $3.00 / $3.09. Which has the larger relative spread, and roughly by how much?
choices: A, because its spread is $0.04 versus $0.09
B, roughly 3% versus 0.016%, so about 190 times larger
They are the same in percentage terms
It cannot be determined without volume
questions.explain: Relative spread is spread divided by price. A: 0.04 / 250 = 0.016%. B: 0.09 / 3.045 = about 3%. The thin stock costs far more to trade in and out of.

questions.q: A quote page shows Previous close 80.00, Open 83.00, Last 83.50. Which statement is correct?
choices: The stock is up $0.50 on the day
The stock gapped up $3.00 at the open and has gained another $0.50 since
The stock is down because it opened above the last price
The day range is $3.50
questions.explain: Change is measured from the previous close: +$3.50 total. Most of it ($3.00) happened in the gap between yesterday's close and today's open.

questions.q: What does a price move on volume well above the stock's average suggest?
choices: The move is probably a data error
More participants are involved, so the move carries more weight
The spread must have widened
The company paid a dividend
questions.explain: Heavy volume means many shares changed hands at those prices. Traders give such moves more credibility than moves on thin volume, though it is a tendency, not a guarantee.

questions.q: How does the paper-trading simulator in this app treat the bid-ask spread?
choices: It fills buys at the ask and sells at the bid using live quotes
It adds a fixed 1% spread to every order
It ignores the spread and fills everything at the last price, so real results will be slightly worse
It only models the spread for options
questions.explain: Paper fills happen at the last price with no spread. Expect real trading to cost a little more on every round trip.

questions.q: A stock is trading at $30.00. You want to buy only if it dips to $29.00 or lower. Which order do you place?
choices: Market buy
Buy limit at $29.00
Buy stop at $29.00
Sell stop at $29.00
questions.explain: A buy limit executes only at the limit price or better (lower). A buy stop at $29 makes no sense because stops trigger when price moves toward them from the other side; a buy stop belongs above the current price.

questions.q: You own shares bought at $80 and place a sell stop at $74. The stock closes at $75 and opens the next day at $66 after bad news. What most likely happens?
choices: You are sold at $74 as the stop promised
The stop triggers at the open and you are sold near $66
The stop is cancelled because the price skipped it
The stop converts to a limit order at $74
questions.explain: A stop becomes a market order once price reaches or passes the stop level. After a gap it fills at the next available price, here around $66. Stops do not protect against gaps.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of a stop-limit order compared with a plain stop?
choices: It costs a higher commission
It avoids a bad fill after a gap but may not fill at all, leaving you in the position
It fills faster
It can only be used to buy
questions.explain: When triggered, a stop-limit becomes a limit order, so it will not sell below your limit. If the price gaps through the limit you simply remain unfilled.

questions.q: In the paper-trading engine, when does an open sell limit at $120 fill?
choices: When any bar's high is at or above $120
When any bar's low is at or below $120
Only when the close is exactly $120
Immediately, at the current price
questions.explain: A sell limit asks for $120 or better. The engine fills it when a bar's range reaches that price from below, that is, when the high touches or exceeds $120.

questions.q: What does a time in force of 'day' mean?
choices: The order can only be placed during daylight hours
The order fills at the day's closing price
The order is cancelled at the end of the trading session if it has not filled
The order remains open for 24 hours
questions.explain: Day orders expire at the close. GTC (good 'til cancelled) orders stay open across sessions until filled or cancelled.

questions.q: Most US brokers charge no commission on stock trades. Which of these is a real way they earn money instead?
choices: A share of each company's profits
Interest on customers' uninvested cash, margin loans, and payment for order flow
Fees paid by the exchanges for listing stocks
Government subsidies
questions.explain: Zero-commission brokers earn interest on cash balances, charge interest on margin, and often receive payment for order flow from wholesalers who execute customer orders.

questions.q: Which of these does paper trading NOT realistically teach?
choices: How order types fill
How to read a profit-and-loss statement
The emotional pressure of losing real money
How to keep a trading journal
questions.explain: Simulated losses do not hurt, so paper trading cannot reproduce the fear and impatience that cause most real-money mistakes. The mechanics and process skills do transfer.

questions.q: A company reports quarterly earnings of $3.10 per share, a record, against a published estimate of $3.00. The stock falls 7%. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The data provider made an error
Record earnings are always bad for a stock
Traders had bid the price up in anticipation of an even better result, so the report disappointed relative to what was priced in
The company must have cut its dividend
questions.explain: Prices move on the gap between results and expectations. If the run-up before the report implied something better than $3.10, a record quarter can still be a letdown.

questions.q: Interest rates are expected to rise. Which effect on stocks is most commonly described?
choices: Stocks, especially fast-growing ones, tend to fall because future profits are worth less today and bonds become more competitive
Stocks always rise because banks earn more
There is no connection between rates and stocks
Only dividend stocks are affected
questions.explain: Higher rates raise the discount applied to future earnings and make safer bonds relatively more attractive. Growth stocks, whose value lies far in the future, are usually most sensitive. It is a tendency, not a law.

questions.q: Under the US pattern day trader rule, what happens if you make four or more day trades in five business days in a margin account below $25,000?
choices: You owe a tax penalty
Your account is flagged and restricted from further day trading until you add funds
Your broker must pay you payment for order flow
Nothing; the rule only applies to options
questions.explain: The rule flags frequent day trading in small margin accounts and restricts it. It is one reason many students prefer holding trades for several days (swing trading) while learning.

questions.q: A daily candle has open $250.00, high $254.10, low $248.60 and close $253.20. How tall is the body?
questions.explain: The body runs from the open to the close: 253.20 − 250.00 = $3.20. The full range (high − low) is $5.50; the upper wick is $0.90 and the lower wick is $1.40.

questions.q: A stock closed yesterday at $100, opened today at $104 and closed today at $102. What colour is today's candle?
choices: Green, because the stock is up 2% on the day
Red, because the close is below the open
Green, because the close is above yesterday's close
It depends on the volume
questions.explain: Candle colour compares the close with the open of the same candle. 102 is below 104, so the candle is red even though the stock gained versus yesterday's close.

questions.q: Which candle shape best describes 'sellers pushed price down hard but buyers took it all back by the close'?
choices: A long red body with no wicks
A tiny body with a long upper wick
A small body near the top with a long lower wick
A doji with equal wicks
questions.explain: A long lower wick means price traded well below the body and then recovered. A small body near the top of the range shows the recovery held into the close.

questions.q: How many 5-minute candles fit in one regular US trading session (9:30 to 16:00 Eastern)?
questions.explain: The regular session is 6.5 hours = 390 minutes. 390 ÷ 5 = 78 candles.

questions.q: Which timeframe is the most sensible main chart for someone who expects to hold a position for a few weeks?
choices: 1-minute
5-minute
Daily
Whichever shows the most trades
questions.explain: The timeframe should match the holding period. Daily candles show a multi-week position's progress without the noise of intraday swings; a 1- or 5-minute chart would prompt reactions to movements that are irrelevant at that horizon.

questions.q: A stock's swing points, in order, are 100, 110, 105, 118, 112, 125. What trend does this describe?
choices: Downtrend: the pullbacks are getting bigger
Uptrend: higher highs (110, 118, 125) and higher lows (105, 112)
Sideways range between 100 and 125
Not enough information
questions.explain: Each swing high (110 → 118 → 125) is higher than the last and each swing low (105 → 112) is higher than the last. That is the definition of an uptrend.

questions.q: By the swing-point definition, when is an uptrend considered broken?
choices: When a single red candle appears
When price closes below the most recent swing low
When the stock falls 1% from its high
When volume declines for three days
questions.explain: An uptrend is a series of higher lows. A break below the most recent swing low means that sequence has failed. Red candles and small declines happen inside every uptrend.

questions.q: A stock has bounced at $148.20, $149.60 and $150.10 on three occasions. What is the best description of its support?
choices: Exactly $149.30, the average of the three
A zone roughly from $148 to $150
$150.10, the most recent bounce
There is no support because the prices differ
questions.explain: Support and resistance are zones, not precise lines. Three bounces within about two dollars define an area; demanding precision to the penny leads to being stopped out by noise.

questions.q: A stock struggled at $200 resistance for two months, then rallied to $215. According to the polarity principle, what is $200 likely to act as now?
choices: Resistance, as before
Support
Nothing; old levels stop mattering after a breakout
A guaranteed buy point
questions.explain: Broken resistance often becomes support because breakout buyers defend their entries and latecomers buy the retest. It is likely, not guaranteed: a fall back through $200 would signal a failed breakout.

questions.q: Why do moving averages confirm trends late?
choices: They are computed from future prices
They average past closes, so they reflect where price has been rather than where it is going
They only update once a week
They ignore the open and close
questions.explain: A 50-day moving average is the average of the last 50 closes. It cannot turn until enough recent closes have moved, so it lags price by design. That smoothing is also what makes it useful as a trend filter.

questions.q: A stock makes swing lows at $100 on day 1 and $106 on day 11. If the trend line holds, roughly where will it be on day 21?
questions.explain: The line rises $6 over 10 days, or $0.60 per day. Ten more days adds another $6: 106 + 6 = $112.

questions.q: How many touches are usually required before a trend line is considered confirmed?
choices: One
Two
Three
Ten
questions.explain: Two points are needed to draw any line; a third touch that holds is what shows the market is actually respecting it. One or two touches could easily be coincidence.

questions.q: A rising channel is $10 wide and price breaks above the upper rail at $110. What is the common measured-move target?
questions.explain: The measured-move rule of thumb adds the channel width to the breakout point: 110 + 10 = $120. It is a heuristic for planning, not a guarantee.

questions.q: A stock averages 50 million shares a day and breaks out above resistance on 52 million shares. How should you read the volume?
choices: Strong confirmation: volume was above average
Weak confirmation: volume was essentially normal
Bearish: breakouts should happen on low volume
Volume is irrelevant for breakouts
questions.explain: 52 million is only 4% above average, which is noise. Convincing breakouts usually come with volume well above normal (many traders look for 1.5x to 2x or more), showing broad participation.

questions.q: Three 5-minute candles trade 10,000 shares at $100.00, 30,000 at $100.50 and 20,000 at $100.20. What is the VWAP?
questions.explain: Total dollars = 1,000,000 + 3,015,000 + 2,004,000 = 6,019,000; total shares = 60,000; 6,019,000 ÷ 60,000 = $100.32. The unweighted average ($100.23) is lower because it ignores that most shares traded at $100.50.

questions.q: A candle has a range of $4.00 from low to high. At most how large can its body be for the dashboard to classify it as a doji?
questions.explain: The detector calls a candle a doji when the body is 10% or less of the range: 10% of $4.00 is $0.40.

questions.q: After a week of declines a stock opens at $97.80, falls to $94.10 and closes at $98.00 (the high). What pattern is this?
choices: Shooting star
Bearish engulfing
Hammer
Doji
questions.explain: A small body ($0.20) at the top of the range with a long lower wick ($3.70) after a decline is a hammer: sellers pushed down hard and buyers took it all back.

questions.q: Why is a hammer-shaped candle in the middle of a sideways range NOT considered a hammer signal?
choices: Hammers only occur on weekly charts
A reversal pattern needs a prior trend to reverse
Sideways ranges have no wicks
The body must be green in a range
questions.explain: The hammer's story is that a decline was rejected. Without a decline leading into it, the same shape is just a candle with a long lower wick; the dashboard's detector will not label it.

questions.q: Day one: a red candle from $100.00 to $98.00. Day two: a green candle from $97.50 to $101.00. What is this?
choices: Morning star
Piercing line
Bullish engulfing
Three white soldiers
questions.explain: The green body (97.50 to 101.00) opens below the red close and closes above the red open, completely covering the previous body in the opposite colour: a bullish engulfing pattern.

questions.q: What does it mean for a shooting star to be 'confirmed'?
choices: The same shape appears again the next day
Volume was below average
The next candle closes below the shooting star's low
The RSI is above 70
questions.explain: Confirmation means the following candle resolves the indecision in the pattern's direction. For a bearish shooting star that is a close below its low; for a bullish hammer, a close above its high.

questions.q: In a head and shoulders top the head peaks at $120 and the neckline is at $100. What is the measured-move target after a neckline break?
questions.explain: The pattern height is 120 − 100 = $20. Project that distance down from the neckline break: 100 − 20 = $80. Targets are planning tools, not guarantees.

questions.q: A stock peaks at $150, drops to $138, rallies to $149.20 and turns down. When does this become a confirmed double top?
choices: As soon as the second peak fails below $150
When price closes below the $138 trough
When volume declines
When the RSI crosses 50
questions.explain: Two peaks alone are only a potential pattern. The double top completes when price closes below the trough between the peaks ($138). Until then the stock may simply be in a range that resolves upward.

questions.q: Which of these is a continuation pattern?
choices: Head and shoulders top
Double bottom
Bull flag
Triple top
questions.explain: A flag is a brief pause after a sharp move, after which the prior trend is expected to resume. Head and shoulders, double bottoms and triple tops are reversal patterns.

questions.q: A stock rallies from $20 to $25, consolidates in a flag down to $23.50, then breaks out at $25.20. What is the measured-move target?
questions.explain: The pole is 25 − 20 = $5. Adding the pole height to the breakout point gives 25.20 + 5.00 = $30.20.

questions.q: A triangle has a flat top with repeated highs near $60 and rising lows. What is it called, and which way does it usually lean?
choices: Descending triangle, bearish lean
Ascending triangle, bullish lean
Symmetrical triangle, neutral
Rising wedge, bearish lean
questions.explain: A flat top with rising lows is an ascending triangle: buyers step in earlier each time while sellers hold a fixed line, so the expected (not guaranteed) resolution is upward.

questions.q: The last five daily closes are $40, $42, $41, $44 and $43. What is the 5-day simple moving average?
questions.explain: Add the five closes (40 + 42 + 41 + 44 + 43 = 210) and divide by 5: $42.00. Every close gets equal weight in a simple moving average.

questions.q: What is the smoothing constant k for a 9-period exponential moving average?
questions.explain: k = 2 / (n + 1) = 2 / 10 = 0.20. Each new close gets 20% of the weight; the previous EMA carries the other 80%.

questions.q: Yesterday's 9-period EMA was $50.00 and today's close is $55.00. What is today's EMA?
questions.explain: EMA = 55 × 0.20 + 50 × 0.80 = 11 + 40 = $51.00. The EMA moved $1 on a $5 jump, faster than a 9-day SMA would have (about $0.56).

questions.q: In which kind of market does a moving-average crossover system typically lose money through repeated small losses?
choices: A strong uptrend
A strong downtrend
A sideways, range-bound market
A market with high volume
questions.explain: In a range the fast average crosses the slow one back and forth, generating buys near the top and sells near the bottom: the whipsaw. Crossovers need a trend to pay off.

questions.q: Which pair of averages does the Broward Trading composite signal use for its crossover component?
choices: SMA 50 and SMA 200
EMA 9 and EMA 21
SMA 20 and SMA 50
SMA 10 and SMA 30
questions.explain: The dashboard scores a golden or death cross of SMA 20 over SMA 50 at ±2 points on the bar it occurs, and ±1 for alignment afterwards. The classic news-headline golden cross is 50 over 200.

questions.q: Over the last 14 days a stock averaged a $0.90 gain on up-days and a $0.30 loss on down-days. What is its RSI?
questions.explain: RS = 0.90 / 0.30 = 3. RSI = 100 − 100 / (1 + 3) = 100 − 25 = 75. Gains three times the size of losses put RSI firmly in the overbought zone.

questions.q: A stock makes a higher high in price while RSI makes a lower high. What is this called and what does it suggest?
choices: Bullish divergence; the uptrend is strengthening
Bearish divergence; upward momentum is fading
A failure swing; buy immediately
A golden cross; the trend has confirmed
questions.explain: Price up, momentum down is bearish divergence. It warns that the rally is being driven with less force, raising the odds of a pullback, though it does not time the turn.

questions.q: Over the last 14 bars the highest high was $84 and the lowest low $76. Today closed at $82. What is the stochastic %K?
questions.explain: %K = 100 × (82 − 76) / (84 − 76) = 100 × 6 / 8 = 75. The close sits three quarters of the way up the recent range.

questions.q: How many points does the composite signal award when RSI is 26?
choices: 0, because 26 is only mildly oversold
questions.explain: RSI below 30 scores +2, the heaviest single weight in the composite. Above 70 scores −2; anywhere between scores 0.

questions.q: Why does a simple "buy below RSI 30" strategy tend to fail in a strong downtrend?
choices: RSI cannot be computed when prices fall
RSI stays oversold for long stretches while price keeps falling, so each buy is early
Downtrends have no volume
RSI only works on weekly charts
questions.explain: Oversold describes a stretched rate of decline, not a floor. In a persistent downtrend RSI can stay below 30 for weeks, and every buy is a bet against the trend. A trend filter such as price versus SMA 50 is the usual fix.

questions.q: EMA 12 is $48.60 and EMA 26 is $47.40. The signal line is at 0.90. What is the MACD histogram?
questions.explain: MACD = 48.60 − 47.40 = 1.20. Histogram = MACD − signal = 1.20 − 0.90 = +0.30. Positive histogram means the MACD line is above its signal line.

questions.q: The 20-day SMA is $80 and the standard deviation of the last 20 closes is $3. Where are the standard Bollinger Bands?
questions.explain: Standard bands are the middle ± 2 standard deviations: 80 ± 6, so $74 and $86. Bandwidth is 12 / 80 = 15%.

questions.q: A stock closed at $100 yesterday. Today its high is $99 and its low is $95. What is today's true range?
questions.explain: True range is the largest of high − low ($4), |high − prev close| ($1) and |low − prev close| ($5). The gap down from $100 to the $95 low is the biggest distance, so TR = $5.

questions.q: You will risk $600 on a trade. Entry is $42 and ATR is $1.50. Using a 2 × ATR stop, how many shares do you buy?
questions.explain: Stop distance = 2 × 1.50 = $3.00. Shares = 600 / 3 = 200. The stop goes at $39.00.

questions.q: Price closes above the upper Bollinger Band right after a multi-month squeeze in bandwidth. How does a trend trader read this?
choices: A sell signal, because price is overbought
A breakout with expanding volatility, likely the start of a move
A signal to switch to a 50-day band
Nothing; band tags are random
questions.explain: A squeeze means volatility was unusually low; the first close outside the bands after a squeeze is read as the start of an expansion, not a reversion. The composite signal still scores it −1, which is one reason to read the context, not just the score.

questions.q: +DI is 35 and −DI is 15 on a daily chart. What is the directional index (DX) for that bar, before smoothing?
questions.explain: DX = 100 × |35 − 15| / (35 + 15) = 100 × 20 / 50 = 40. Smoothing this over 14 bars gives ADX; the DI lines themselves give direction (buyers lead here).

questions.q: ADX reads 42 on a stock. Which statement is correct?
choices: The stock is in a strong uptrend
The stock is in a strong downtrend
The stock is in a strong trend; check +DI vs −DI for direction
The stock is overbought
questions.explain: ADX measures strength only. A high ADX can accompany a rally or a collapse. +DI above −DI means up; −DI above +DI means down.

questions.q: Three 5-minute bars after the open: typical prices $50, $51, $52 with volumes 20,000, 10,000 and 10,000. What is VWAP?
questions.explain: VWAP = (50 × 20,000 + 51 × 10,000 + 52 × 10,000) / 40,000 = 2,030,000 / 40,000 = $50.75. The heavy volume at $50 pulls it below the simple average of $51.

questions.q: In the Ichimoku system, how is Senkou Span B calculated and where is it drawn?
choices: 9-bar midpoint, drawn on the current bar
Average of Tenkan and Kijun, drawn 26 bars ahead
52-bar midpoint of the high–low range, drawn 26 bars ahead
Today's close, drawn 26 bars back
questions.explain: Senkou B is the midpoint of the 52-bar range, shifted 26 bars forward. Senkou A is the Tenkan/Kijun average shifted forward; the Chikou is the close shifted back.

questions.q: ADX is 15 on the daily chart. Which family of strategies does this reading favour?
choices: Moving-average crossovers
Channel breakouts
Mean-reversion tools such as RSI reversion or Bollinger bounce
None; trading is impossible below ADX 20
questions.explain: An ADX below 20 is the classic rule-of-thumb signature of a range. Trend tools whipsaw in ranges; fading the extremes has the better odds. The thresholds are conventions, not laws, but the direction of the advice is widely agreed.

questions.q: Which set of indicators draws from four different families and so gives the least redundant picture?
choices: RSI, stochastic, MACD histogram, CCI
SMA 50, RSI, ATR, ADX
EMA 9, EMA 21, SMA 50, SMA 200
Bollinger Bands, ATR, bandwidth, standard deviation
questions.explain: SMA 50 is trend, RSI is momentum, ATR is volatility and ADX is regime. The other sets are four versions of one family and will agree with each other almost by construction.

questions.q: Close is above SMA 50, SMA 20 is above SMA 50, RSI is 27, the MACD histogram is positive and rising, the close is inside the Bollinger Bands, and no cross happened this bar. What does the composite score?
choices: +3, BUY
+4, BUY
+5, BUY
+2, HOLD
questions.explain: +1 (price vs SMA 50) +1 (alignment) +2 (RSI oversold) +1 (histogram positive and rising) +0 (inside bands) +0 (no cross) = +5, a BUY.

questions.q: Price is below a falling SMA 50, SMA 20 is below SMA 50, RSI is 73, the MACD histogram is positive and rising, and the close is above the upper Bollinger Band. What is the score and state?
choices: −2, HOLD
−3, SELL
−4, SELL
0, HOLD
questions.explain: −1 (below SMA 50) −1 (bearish alignment) −2 (RSI overbought) +1 (histogram rising) −1 (above upper band) = −4, SELL. A sharp bounce in a downtrend is exactly what the mean-reversion components flag.

questions.q: Which of these does the composite signal NOT take into account?
choices: The 50-bar simple moving average
The RSI zone
Trading volume
The MACD histogram
questions.explain: None of the six scored rules use volume. ADX and candlestick patterns are shown as zero-point context; volume is not shown at all, so you must read it yourself from the volume bars or VWAP.

questions.q: The badge showed BUY at +5 yesterday and +3 today, yet the chart looks unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: RSI must have risen above 70
The golden cross bonus (+2) counts only on the bar it occurs
The data provider changed
ADX dropped below 20 and removed two points
questions.explain: Component 6 scores an event: ±2 on the single bar where SMA 20 crosses SMA 50. The next day the alignment still earns +1 but the cross bonus is gone, so the score falls by 2 with no change in the picture. ADX never adds or removes points.

questions.q: Your account equity is $100,000 and you risk 1% per trade. You buy a stock at $80 with a stop at $76. How many shares should you buy?
choices: 1,250 shares
250 shares
100 shares
25 shares
questions.explain: Risk budget is $1,000. Stop distance is 80 − 76 = $4. $1,000 ÷ $4 = 250 shares, a $20,000 position. 1,250 shares would put the whole account into one stock.

questions.q: You tighten your stop from $4 below entry to $1 below entry and keep the same 1% risk budget. What happens to the share count?
choices: It falls to a quarter, making the trade safer
It stays the same
It quadruples; the dollar risk is unchanged but the stop is far more likely to be hit
It cannot be calculated without knowing the ATR
questions.explain: Shares = risk ÷ distance. Dividing the distance by four multiplies the share count by four. The planned dollar loss is still 1%, but a stop one dollar away sits inside normal daily noise and will be triggered far more often.

questions.q: Stock A has an ATR of $1 and stock B an ATR of $4, both at $100. Using a 2-ATR stop and the same risk budget, how do the position sizes compare?
choices: Equal, because the prices are equal
A gets four times as many shares as B
B gets four times as many shares as A
A gets twice as many shares as B
questions.explain: A's stop distance is $2 and B's is $8. The same risk budget divided by a distance one quarter as large gives four times the shares. Volatility-adjusted sizing equalises the dollar risk, not the share count.

questions.q: Why is the 1% rule described as a rule of thumb rather than a fixed law?
choices: Because it only applies to accounts over $1,000,000
Because practitioners disagree: many institutional desks use well under 1% and some books suggest up to 2%; the shared idea is that a losing streak must not be fatal
Because the SEC sets the correct figure each year
Because it only matters for day traders
questions.explain: There is no single correct number. The arithmetic of losing streaks argues for small per-trade risk, and most guidance lands between 0.25% and 2%. The 1% figure is a sensible default for learning.

questions.q: You hold six positions each risking 1%, all large-cap technology stocks. What is the main problem?
choices: Nothing; each position is correctly sized
Portfolio heat is 6% and the positions are highly correlated, so a sector selloff can hit every stop at once
Six positions is too few for diversification
Technology stocks cannot be stopped out
questions.explain: Correctly sizing each trade does not protect you from six correlated trades losing together. Capping total open risk and treating same-sector names as one position for heat purposes are the standard fixes.

questions.q: You buy at $60 with a stop at $57 and a target at $66. What is the trade's reward in R?
choices: 1R
2R
3R
questions.explain: R is the risk per share, 60 − 57 = $3. The target is $6 above entry, which is 6 ÷ 3 = 2R. The risk/reward is 1:2.

questions.q: What is the break-even win rate for a strategy whose winners are always 3R and losers always 1R, ignoring costs?
questions.explain: Break-even = 1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%. At a 25% win rate, one 3R win pays for three 1R losses exactly.

questions.q: A trader wins 65% of trades, with average winner 0.6R and average loser 1.4R. What is the expectancy?
questions.explain: 0.65 × 0.6 = 0.39R from winners; 0.35 × 1.4 = 0.49R lost on losers. 0.39 − 0.49 = −0.10R per trade. A high win rate cannot rescue a bad payoff ratio.

questions.q: Which of these is the recommended way to set a stop?
choices: Decide the share count first, then put the stop where the loss equals your budget
Put the stop where the chart shows the trade idea has failed, then size the position from that distance
Always use exactly 5% below entry
Set it after the trade starts losing, once you know how it feels
questions.explain: The stop should mark where the thesis is wrong (below support, a swing low, or an ATR multiple). The share count is then derived from the stop distance and the risk budget, never the other way round.

questions.q: A backtest shows a profit factor of 1.8 on 11 trades. What is the most important caution?
choices: 1.8 is too low to be interesting
Eleven trades is far too small a sample; the number could easily reverse on the next dozen trades
Profit factor must be above 3 to count
Backtests cannot compute profit factor
questions.explain: Small samples are dominated by chance. A genuine edge can show losing stretches of a dozen trades and a worthless strategy can show winning ones. Thirty trades is a bare minimum, and more is better.

questions.q: An account falls from a peak of $120,000 to $90,000. What is the drawdown, and what gain is needed to recover?
choices: 25% drawdown; 25% gain
25% drawdown; 33.3% gain
33% drawdown; 25% gain
30% drawdown; 30% gain
questions.explain: Drawdown = 30,000 ÷ 120,000 = 25%. Recovery needs 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 33.3%, because the gain is measured on the smaller base of $90,000.

questions.q: With a 50% win rate, roughly how likely is it that a trader sees at least one run of five consecutive losses somewhere in 100 trades?
choices: About 3%
About 20%
About 80%
Essentially impossible
questions.explain: Any single five-trade window has a 1-in-32 chance of being all losers, but there are nearly 100 overlapping windows in 100 trades. The chance of at least one such streak is roughly 80%. Streaks are normal.

questions.q: After three losing trades in a row, a trader doubles the size of the next trade to get back to even quickly. Which bias is this?
choices: Confirmation bias
Recency bias
Revenge trading
The disposition effect
questions.explain: Increasing size after losses to win back the money is revenge trading. It turns a normal, survivable streak into a large drawdown. A fixed daily loss limit is the usual defence.

questions.q: What did Odean's 1998 study of brokerage accounts find?
choices: Investors held winners too long and sold losers quickly
Investors were more likely to sell stocks that had risen than stocks that had fallen, and the stocks they sold went on to outperform the ones they kept
Investors who traded more earned more
Stop losses were used by most retail investors
questions.explain: This is the disposition effect: selling winners and holding losers. It is the practical face of loss aversion and the opposite of the payoff profile that produces positive expectancy.

questions.q: Why does sizing at 1% per trade help with losing streaks specifically?
choices: It prevents streaks from happening
It guarantees a 1% return per trade
Ten consecutive 1% losses cost under 10% of equity, keeping the account in the gentle part of the recovery curve, whereas ten 5% losses cost about 40%
It is required by exchanges
questions.explain: Streaks cannot be prevented, only survived. Small per-trade risk keeps the inevitable streak from pushing the account into drawdowns that need huge gains to recover.

questions.q: You short 200 shares at $40 and cover at $46. Ignoring fees, what is your result?
questions.explain: A short profits when price falls. Here price rose $6, so you lost $6 × 200 = $1,200. Covering higher than you sold is a loss.

questions.q: Under US Regulation T, roughly how much of your own money must back a $20,000 short sale at initiation?
choices: $0, because the sale proceeds cover it
$10,000, so that total collateral is 150% of the short value
questions.explain: The requirement is 150% of the short's value: the $20,000 proceeds plus 50% ($10,000) of your own equity. The paper account applies the same 150% cash rule.

questions.q: You buy $100,000 of stock with $50,000 cash and $50,000 of margin. The stock falls 15%. What happens to your equity?
choices: It falls 15% to $42,500
It falls 30% to $35,000
It falls 7.5% to $46,250
It is unchanged because the broker takes the loss
questions.explain: The position is worth $85,000 and you still owe $50,000, so equity is $35,000: a 30% loss on your money. Two-times leverage doubles the percentage move in both directions.

questions.q: What order type is the short seller's equivalent of a stop loss?
choices: A sell stop below the entry
A buy stop above the entry, which triggers if price rises to that level
A buy limit below the entry
Shorts cannot use stops
questions.explain: A short loses as price rises, so the protective order is a buy stop placed above entry. When price reaches it, the order buys to cover and caps the loss (gaps aside).

questions.q: Why is the maximum loss on a short position described as unlimited?
choices: Because brokers charge unlimited fees
Because a stock's price has no upper bound, so the cost to buy back the borrowed shares can rise without limit, as in a short squeeze
Because short positions can never be closed
Because the SEC requires it
questions.explain: A long can only fall to zero. A short's loss grows with the price, which has no ceiling. Squeezes such as Volkswagen in 2008 and GameStop in 2021 show how far and how fast that can go.

questions.q: Which of these is a testable entry rule suitable for a trading plan?
choices: Buy when the stock looks strong
Buy when the news is good
Buy when price closes above the 20-day SMA after a pullback to a rising 50-day SMA with RSI between 40 and 60
Buy whenever a friend recommends it
questions.explain: A plan rule must be specific enough that two people would agree whether it fired on a given chart, and that it can be journalled and backtested. Only the third option meets that standard.

questions.q: What is the single most valuable column in a trading journal, according to this lesson?
choices: The stock's sector
Whether you followed the plan on that trade
The time of day
Your mood before the market opened
questions.explain: Splitting trades into plan-following and plan-breaking and computing expectancy for each shows whether the method or the discipline is the problem, and puts a dollar figure on rule breaks.

questions.q: A learner trades a $100,000 paper account with $40,000 positions, even though they plan to start live with $5,000. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing; the paper money is not real
They are not learning to operate at the size and constraints they will actually face, so the habits will not transfer
Paper accounts cannot hold positions over $10,000
Positions must always be exactly 1% of equity
questions.explain: Paper trading only builds useful habits if it mirrors the real account. Resetting the paper account to the intended live size and sizing at 1% of that is the recommended approach.

questions.q: Why should promising backtest or paper results be re-checked with commission and slippage turned on?
choices: Because costs subtract directly from expectancy and can turn a small edge into a loss, especially for frequent trading
Because the regulator requires it
Because commission increases win rate
Because slippage only affects short positions
questions.explain: Every trade pays costs regardless of outcome. A strategy with a thin per-trade expectancy can have none left after realistic commissions and slippage, which is why high-frequency approaches often fail live.

questions.q: A profitable 40-trade record was built entirely while the dashboard showed the Demo data badge. What does this prove about the strategy?
choices: That it will be profitable live
That it beats buy and hold
Very little about the strategy: demo prices are a simulated random walk, so the record only shows the mechanics were practised
That the 1% rule is unnecessary
questions.explain: Demo data is generated, not real. It is ideal for learning order entry, sizing and journalling, but a profitable record on it says nothing about an edge in real markets. Use a real data source for that.

questions.q: A stock trades at $52. You buy one $50 call for a premium of $3.10. How much cash leaves your account, and what is the option's intrinsic value?
choices: $3.10 leaves; intrinsic value is $2.00
$310 leaves; intrinsic value is $2.00 per share
$310 leaves; intrinsic value is $3.10 per share
$5,000 leaves; intrinsic value is zero
questions.explain: One standard contract covers 100 shares, so a $3.10 premium costs $310. Intrinsic value for a call is stock price minus strike when positive: 52 − 50 = $2.00 per share. The other $1.10 of the premium is extrinsic (time) value.

questions.q: Which position has an obligation rather than a right?
choices: Long call
Long put
Short put
None of them; all options are rights
questions.explain: Buying a call or a put gives you a right. Selling (writing) an option gives the buyer a right over you, so the short put carries the obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike if assigned.

questions.q: A stock is at $80. Which option is in the money?
choices: The $85 call
The $75 put
The $85 put
The $80 call
questions.explain: A put is in the money when its strike is above the stock price: the $85 put has 85 − 80 = $5 of intrinsic value. The $85 call and $75 put are out of the money, and the $80 call is at the money with zero intrinsic value.

questions.q: You own a call that is $4 in the money with 20 days left and a market price of $5.20. Which is the best way to take your profit?
choices: Exercise it now to lock in the $4
Sell the call in the market for $5.20
Wait for automatic exercise at expiration
Buy a put at the same strike
questions.explain: Exercising captures only the $4 of intrinsic value and throws away $1.20 of extrinsic value. Selling the contract captures the full $5.20. Waiting exposes you to 20 more days of price risk and time decay.

questions.q: What happens at expiration to an equity option that finishes $0.30 in the money if the holder gives no instructions?
choices: It expires worthless because the amount is too small
The clearing house automatically exercises it
It is converted to cash equal to the premium paid
It rolls to the next expiration automatically
questions.explain: The OCC automatically exercises equity options that finish in the money by $0.01 or more unless the holder opts out. The holder ends up long (call) or short (put) 100 shares per contract, which is why traders close positions before expiration if they do not want the shares.

questions.q: On an option chain in the standard layout, where are the puts?
choices: Above the calls, sorted by expiration
To the right of the strike column, with calls on the left
In a separate table you must open
Mixed with calls, sorted by price
questions.explain: The conventional chain puts calls on the left, strikes in the centre column and puts on the right, one row per strike. The Options Lab uses the same layout.

questions.q: A call shows bid $1.80 and ask $2.20. You buy at the ask and the stock does not move. If you sold back immediately, roughly what would you lose per contract?
questions.explain: Buying at $2.20 and selling at the $1.80 bid loses $0.40 per share, and a contract covers 100 shares, so $40. The bid-ask spread is the first cost of every options trade.

questions.q: What does the contract symbol MSFT250919P00400000 describe?
choices: A Microsoft $400 call expiring 19 September 2025
A Microsoft $400 put expiring 19 September 2025
A Microsoft $40 put expiring 25 September 2019
A Microsoft $4,000 put expiring 19 September 2025
questions.explain: The format is root, YYMMDD, C or P, then strike × 1000 as eight digits. 250919 is 19 September 2025, P means put, and 00400000 ÷ 1000 = $400.

questions.q: A stock is at $60. You buy the $65 call for $1.20. What is the breakeven price at expiration?
questions.explain: For a long call, breakeven at expiration is strike plus premium: 65 + 1.20 = $66.20. The stock must rise more than 10% for the position to make money if held to expiration.

questions.q: Which statement about open interest is most accurate?
choices: High open interest at a strike means the stock will be pinned there
Open interest is the number of contracts traded today
Open interest is a liquidity indicator showing how many contracts are outstanding
Open interest only counts contracts bought by retail traders
questions.explain: Open interest counts contracts currently outstanding and is updated overnight. It is useful as a liquidity signal (tighter spreads where OI is high). Volume is today's traded count. Treating OI as a price forecast is a common mistake.

questions.q: A call has a delta of 0.40 and costs $2.00. The stock rises $1. Ignoring other effects, roughly what is the call now worth?
questions.explain: Delta is the price change per $1 move in the stock: 0.40 × $1 = $0.40, so the call goes to about $2.40. Gamma would then raise the delta slightly for the next dollar.

questions.q: Which option has the highest gamma?
choices: A deep in-the-money call with 120 days to expiration
A far out-of-the-money put with 120 days to expiration
An at-the-money call with 5 days to expiration
An at-the-money call with 120 days to expiration
questions.explain: Gamma peaks at the money and rises sharply as expiration approaches. Short-dated at-the-money options have the highest gamma, which is why their deltas swing so violently on small moves.

questions.q: Theta on a long option is −0.08. What does that mean?
choices: The option gains $0.08 per day as expiration nears
The option loses about $0.08 per share, or $8 per contract, per day if nothing else changes
The option loses 8% of its value every day
The option will be worth $0.08 at expiration
questions.explain: Theta is the model's estimate of daily decay in extrinsic value per share, all else equal. Multiply by 100 for the per-contract dollar amount. It is a dollar figure, not a percentage, and it grows as expiration approaches for at-the-money options.

questions.q: A trader buys a call the day before earnings at 70% implied volatility. The stock rises 3% after the report, but IV drops to 35%. What most likely happened to the call's value?
choices: It rose by exactly the delta times the move
It may have fallen, because the loss from vega can exceed the gain from delta
It doubled, because IV always boosts calls
Nothing, because IV only affects puts
questions.explain: This is IV crush. The option's price included a large volatility premium that disappeared after the event. A near-dated call can lose more from the IV collapse (vega) than it gains from a modest move in the stock (delta), so the trader can be right on direction and still lose.

questions.q: A $50 stock has 40% implied volatility. Roughly what is the one-standard-deviation expected move over 30 days?
choices: About $1.60
About $5.70
About $20.00
About $0.40
questions.explain: Expected move ≈ price × IV × √(days ÷ 365) = 50 × 0.40 × √(30 ÷ 365) ≈ 50 × 0.40 × 0.287 ≈ $5.73. The $20 answer is the full-year move (50 × 0.40) and ignores the time scaling.

questions.q: You own 100 shares bought at $48 and sell a $50 call for $1.20. The stock closes at $56 at expiration. What is your profit?
questions.explain: You are assigned and sell at $50: ($50 − $48) × 100 = $200, plus the $120 premium = $320. You gave up the move above $50 in exchange for the premium; that is the covered-call trade-off.

questions.q: You own 100 shares at $70 and buy a $65 put for $2.00. What is the maximum loss on the combined position at expiration?
questions.explain: The put lets you sell at $65 no matter how far the stock falls, so the stock loss is capped at $5 per share. Add the $2 premium: ($70 − $65 + $2) × 100 = $700.

questions.q: A bull call spread buys the $40 call for $3.00 and sells the $45 call for $1.20. What are the max loss and max profit?
choices: Max loss $180; max profit $320
Max loss $300; max profit $500
Max loss $120; max profit $380
Max loss $180; max profit unlimited
questions.explain: Net debit is $3.00 − $1.20 = $1.80, so max loss is $180. The strike width is $5 ($500 total payoff), so max profit is $500 − $180 = $320. Max loss plus max profit always equals the width times 100.

questions.q: Which strategy profits if the stock stays above a chosen level and loses a limited amount if it falls below a lower level?
choices: Long put
Bull put spread (credit)
Protective put
Long straddle
questions.explain: A bull put spread sells a put and buys a lower-strike put for protection. It keeps the full credit if the stock finishes above the short strike and loses at most the strike width minus the credit.

questions.q: A collar on 100 shares consists of which legs?
choices: Long stock, long call, short put
Long stock, long put, short call
Short stock, long call, long put
Long call and long put at the same strike
questions.explain: A collar protects owned stock with a long put and pays for it (fully or partly) by selling a call above the market. The result is a boxed-in position with a known floor and ceiling.

questions.q: A long straddle buys the $50 call for $2.40 and the $50 put for $2.10. What are the breakevens at expiration?
choices: $50.00 only
questions.explain: Total premium is $2.40 + $2.10 = $4.50. The stock must move more than $4.50 from the $50 strike in either direction: $45.50 or $54.50. Maximum loss ($450) occurs if the stock closes exactly at $50.

questions.q: An iron condor is built with $5-wide wings and collects a $1.40 credit. What is the maximum loss?
questions.explain: Only one wing can be in the money at expiration, and its worst case is the $5 width ($500). Subtract the $140 credit collected on the whole position: $500 − $140 = $360.

questions.q: Which situation makes early assignment of a short call most likely?
choices: The call is far out of the money with 60 days left
The call is in the money, the stock goes ex-dividend tomorrow, and the call's remaining extrinsic value is less than the dividend
Implied volatility rises sharply
The stock is halted for news
questions.explain: A call holder captures a dividend only by owning the shares before the ex-dividend date. If the call's extrinsic value is smaller than the dividend, exercising early is rational, so in-the-money short calls are commonly assigned the day before ex-dividend.

questions.q: You hold a $105/$110 bear call spread into expiration. The stock closes at $106.20. Which description is correct?
choices: Both options expire worthless and you keep the credit
You are assigned on the short $105 call and the long $110 call expires worthless, leaving you short 100 shares over the weekend
Both options are automatically exercised against each other, so your risk is unchanged
The broker converts the spread to cash at the credit received
questions.explain: The short $105 call finishes $1.20 in the money and is auto-exercised against you; the long $110 call is out of the money and expires. Your "defined risk" protection is gone and you carry a naked short stock position until you can trade on Monday. Close spreads near the short strike before expiration.

questions.q: What makes a short put "cash-secured"?
choices: The put is bought back the same day
The seller holds enough cash to buy 100 shares at the strike if assigned
The seller also owns a call at the same strike
The put is far out of the money
questions.explain: A cash-secured put is a short put backed by enough cash to take delivery of the shares at the strike price (strike × 100 per contract). It removes the margin and forced-liquidation risk of a naked short put and is the only way a beginner should sell puts.

questions.q: Which of these is a fully specified strategy rather than an idea?
choices: Buy good companies when they are cheap
Buy at the next open after a daily close with RSI(14) below 30; stop 2 ATR below entry; exit at the next open after RSI closes above 70
Buy strong momentum stocks and hold them while they keep going up
Buy when the chart looks oversold
questions.explain: Only the second option tells you exactly when to enter, at what price, where the stop is and when to exit. Two people following it would take the same trades. The others depend on judgment ("good", "cheap", "strong", "looks oversold").

questions.q: A backtest shows a win rate of 38% but a profit overall. Which family does this strategy most likely belong to?
choices: Mean reversion
Trend following
Arbitrage
It must be a bug; a strategy cannot profit with a win rate under 50%
questions.explain: Trend-following rules typically win less than half the time but their winners are much larger than their losers. A strategy is profitable whenever win rate × average win exceeds loss rate × average loss, so a 38% win rate is fine if winners are big enough.

questions.q: Which of the five parts of a complete strategy is missing from this rule: "Buy AAPL on daily bars when the 20 SMA crosses above the 50 SMA, risking 1% of equity with a stop 2 ATR below entry"?
choices: Universe
Entry
Exit when the trade is right
Timeframe
questions.explain: The rule names its universe (AAPL), entry (the cross), stop (2 ATR), size (1%) and timeframe (daily). It never says how a winning trade ends. Without a profit exit or trailing rule, the strategy is incomplete.

questions.q: What is a time stop?
choices: A stop loss that moves closer to price each day
A rule that exits a trade if it has not made progress within a set number of bars
A rule that stops trading after a fixed number of losses
An order that executes at the market close
questions.explain: A time stop frees up capital from trades that are going nowhere, for example "exit if the trade is not up at least 1R after 10 bars". It is a third kind of exit alongside the stop loss and the profit exit.

questions.q: A trend-following backtest reports a 72% win rate. What is the most sensible first reaction?
choices: Celebrate; trend following usually wins about 70% of the time
Be suspicious and check the rules for errors, because trend systems usually win far less than half the time
Increase position size to take advantage of the edge
Ignore the win rate; it never matters
questions.explain: Trend-following rules buy after a move has started and are stopped out often, so win rates of 30% to 45% are typical. A 72% win rate from such a rule is a red flag for a look-ahead bug or a very small, lucky sample, both covered later in this module.

questions.q: An account grows from $100,000 to $150,000 over 3 years. What is the CAGR, approximately?
questions.explain: CAGR = 1.5^(1/3) − 1 ≈ 0.145, or 14.5% per year. Dividing 50% by 3 to get 16.7% ignores compounding; 8.4% would be the answer over 5 years.

questions.q: A strategy has 16 winners averaging +$1,500 and 24 losers averaging −$750. What is its profit factor?
questions.explain: Gross profit is 16 × 1,500 = $24,000; gross loss is 24 × 750 = $18,000. Profit factor = 24,000 ÷ 18,000 = 1.33. (0.40 is the win rate, not the profit factor.)

questions.q: Equity peaks at $120,000 and falls to $96,000 before recovering. What is the maximum drawdown, and what gain is needed to recover?
choices: 20% drawdown; 20% gain to recover
20% drawdown; 25% gain to recover
25% drawdown; 25% gain to recover
24% drawdown; 24% gain to recover
questions.explain: Drawdown = (120,000 − 96,000) ÷ 120,000 = 20%. To climb from $96,000 back to $120,000 requires 24,000 ÷ 96,000 = 25%. Losses always need a larger percentage gain to undo.

questions.q: Daily returns average 0.05% with a standard deviation of 1.0%. Using the lab's method (risk-free rate zero, √252 annualisation), the Sharpe ratio is about:
questions.explain: Sharpe = (0.0005 ÷ 0.01) × √252 = 0.05 × 15.87 ≈ 0.79. This is a perfectly ordinary figure, roughly in the range of a buy-and-hold stock index over the long run.

questions.q: Why does the lab fill a signal at the open of the next bar rather than the close of the bar that generated it?
choices: Because the open is always a better price
Because the close is not known until the bar has ended, so you cannot trade at it after deciding on it
Because brokers only accept orders at the open
Because it makes the backtest results look better
questions.explain: A rule that reads the closing price has to wait for the close to exist. By then that price is gone. The next realistic fill is the following bar's open. Filling at the signal bar's close is a form of look-ahead bias, covered in Lesson 3.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of look-ahead bias?
choices: Filling a buy signal computed from today's close at tomorrow's open
Normalising prices by subtracting the average price over the whole test period before computing a signal
Using a 20-day rolling SMA
Charging commission on every trade
questions.explain: A full-sample average on bar 50 already includes bars 51 onward, so the strategy is using future prices to decide a past trade. Rolling backward-looking windows and next-open fills are both legitimate.

questions.q: Why does backtesting a buy-the-dip strategy on today's largest companies overstate its results?
choices: Large companies have higher commissions
Because every stock in that universe recovered from every dip by definition, while the ones that did not recover are missing
Because large companies never fall 20%
It does not; large-cap results are the most reliable
questions.explain: This is survivorship bias. A universe chosen today excludes the companies that collapsed or were delisted, which are exactly the stocks where buying the dip would have failed.

questions.q: An optimiser tries 100 parameter combinations for a strategy with no real edge. Using a 5% significance threshold, roughly how many would you expect to look significant by chance?
questions.explain: A 5% threshold means about 1 in 20 worthless strategies passes by luck, so about 5 of 100 will look good. This multiple-comparisons effect is the statistical heart of overfitting.

questions.q: A strategy's best in-sample Sharpe is 1.9. On the 30% hold-out it falls to 0.2. The most reasonable conclusion is:
choices: The hold-out period was unusual; trust the in-sample number
The optimiser fitted noise in the in-sample data; the parameters are not trustworthy
The strategy should be traded with larger size to recover
Sharpe ratios are meaningless
questions.explain: A large collapse from in-sample to out-of-sample is the signature of curve fitting. The parameters were chosen to match the past bars, not a repeating pattern.

questions.q: What does walk-forward analysis add over a single in-sample/out-of-sample split?
choices: It uses more parameters
It repeats the optimise-then-test cycle on rolling windows, so the stitched out-of-sample curve was never tuned on itself and the result does not depend on one lucky cut point
It removes the need for a stop loss
It guarantees the strategy will be profitable live
questions.explain: Walk-forward rolls the in-sample window forward, re-optimises, and tests on the following segment each time. The combined out-of-sample curve mimics how a system would really be re-tuned and traded. It is stronger evidence than one split, but still not a guarantee.

questions.q: A stock is quoted bid $50.00 / ask $50.02. You buy at the market and immediately sell at the market. Ignoring commission and slippage, what did the round trip cost per share?
questions.explain: You paid the ask ($50.02) and received the bid ($50.00). The 2-cent spread, 0.04% of the price, is the cost of the round trip. It is paid on every trade whether or not it shows on a statement.

questions.q: Slippage is set to 10 basis points in the lab. What does that do to a buy fill?
choices: Nothing; it only affects sells
The buy fills 0.10% above the bar's open
The buy fills 10% above the bar's open
The buy is delayed by 10 bars
questions.explain: One basis point is 0.01%, so 10 bps is 0.10%. The lab fills buys 0.10% above the next open and sells 0.10% below it, making the round trip cost about 0.20% of the position.

questions.q: Rule B makes 300 round trips a year with an average gross gain of 0.25% per trade. At a round-trip cost of 0.20%, approximately what share of its gross edge goes to costs?
questions.explain: Costs are 0.20 ÷ 0.25 = 80% of the average gross gain, leaving only 0.05% net per trade. Frequent, small-edge strategies are the most vulnerable to cost assumptions.

questions.q: Which change would most directly make a strategy more resistant to transaction costs?
choices: Trading more often to average out the costs
Switching to thinly traded small caps for bigger moves
Trading less often and holding longer so each round trip covers a larger expected move
Removing the stop loss
questions.explain: The cost of a round trip is roughly fixed, so spreading it over a bigger expected move (fewer trades, longer holds, liquid stocks) is the lever that works. More trades and thinner stocks make costs worse.

questions.q: What does forward testing on a paper account reveal that a backtest cannot?
choices: The strategy's CAGR over the last five years
Whether you can actually execute and follow the rules in real time, on data nobody has tuned on
The optimal parameter values
The maximum historical drawdown
questions.explain: Forward testing exposes execution constraints, genuine out-of-sample market behaviour and, above all, your own ability to follow the system during losses. The backtest already gave you the historical statistics.

questions.q: When should the go / no-go criteria for a strategy be written?
choices: After the backtest, so they can be set realistically
Before running any test, so the results are judged against standards not influenced by them
Only if the backtest is profitable
They are unnecessary if the Sharpe ratio is above 1
questions.explain: Criteria set after seeing results are rationalisations. Writing minimum trades, minimum profit factor with costs, maximum drawdown and an out-of-sample requirement in advance is the strongest defence against fooling yourself.

questions.q: Your rule clears every criterion on AAPL but fails on MSFT and AMZN. What is the most defensible conclusion?
choices: Trade it on AAPL only; that is where the edge is
The rule has probably found something specific to AAPL's past price path rather than a general edge, so it is a no-go or needs more evidence
Average the three results and proceed if the average passes
Remove MSFT and AMZN from the universe retroactively
questions.explain: An edge that appears on one symbol and vanishes on two unrelated ones is the signature of a story about that stock, not a repeatable pattern. Dropping the failing symbols after the fact is a form of overfitting the universe.

questions.q: A first capstone strategy fails the profit-factor criterion with costs. What should the student do?
choices: Lower the criterion to match the result
Remove the costs; the rule passes at zero cost
Record the no-go, write a paragraph on which criterion failed and why, and complete the review; this is a complete project
Increase position size to compensate
questions.explain: Rejecting a rule with a clear, written reason is correct process and most of what real strategy research consists of. Changing the criteria or the cost assumptions to rescue a result is exactly the self-deception the project is designed to prevent.

questions.q: Why does the capstone ask you to log signals you did not take?
choices: To make the win rate look better
Because missed signals reveal whether the strategy fits your schedule and temperament, which the backtest cannot show
Because the lab requires it
Missed signals do not need to be logged
questions.explain: Feasibility is part of a strategy. A rule you cannot follow in practice, whether because of timing or nerves, is not a rule you can trade, and the only way to discover that is to record the misses honestly.

questions.q: If the forward-test results are dramatically worse than the backtest, the most likely explanation is:
choices: Paper trading is unrelated to backtesting
The backtest had a flaw such as look-ahead, unrealistic costs or survivorship bias, which the forward test has just exposed
The strategy needs a larger account
The market was closed on key days
questions.explain: Live results are usually somewhat worse than backtests, but a dramatic gap points to a problem in the backtest itself. Finding that out with paper money, before real money, is the entire purpose of forward testing.

questions.q: What is the main thing Market Replay does that a normal chart cannot?
choices: It shows more indicators at once
It hides the bars to the right of the cursor so you decide without hindsight
It uses faster data than the dashboard
It guarantees that stop orders fill at their price
questions.explain: A finished chart shows the future; replay reveals one bar at a time, so your decisions are made with only the information a trader had on that day. Indicators are computed from revealed bars only, for the same reason.

questions.q: Which account do replay trades go into?
choices: Your main paper portfolio, the same as the dashboard
A separate 'replay' paper account that is reset for every session
A live brokerage account
No account; replay only draws trades on the chart
questions.explain: Replay uses the same paper engine but a separate account called 'replay', so drills never disturb the record you are building in your main paper portfolio.

questions.q: With intrabar ticks off, a daily bar opens below your resting sell stop. Where does the stop fill?
choices: At the stop price
At the bar's open, because the market skipped the stop price
At the bar's low
It does not fill; stops only work with ticks on
questions.explain: A stop becomes a market order when price trades through it. If the bar gaps past the stop at the open, the first available price is the open, which is the honest treatment of a gap and the reason stops are not guarantees.

questions.q: You finish a drill with a losing scorecard. According to the lesson, when is replaying the same drill a good idea?
choices: Whenever you lose; the goal is a winning scorecard
Never; each drill may only be run once
When you have changed one written rule, so the second run tests the change
Only if you look up the real chart first to see what went wrong
questions.explain: Repeating with a changed rule is an experiment. Repeating to erase a loss teaches you that losses can be undone, which a live account will never do, and peeking at the real chart defeats the purpose of hiding the future.

questions.q: What do the years in drill titles such as 'MSFT 2024' refer to in demo mode?
choices: The exact real prices of that calendar year
Scenario labels for a simulated, deterministic price series that every learner sees identically
Random prices generated fresh each time you open the drill
Live prices delayed by one year
questions.explain: Demo data is simulated and deterministic, so every learner replays the same bars and can compare results. With a market-data key connected, the engine replays real historical bars for the range instead.

questions.q: The 'Ride the trend' drill fails if you make more than three round trips, even if the session is profitable. What is that limit teaching?
choices: That trading costs are the main problem
That most of a trending year's return comes from holding, so churning through pullbacks is the mistake even when it happens to work
That the engine cannot process more than three trades
That you should always use buy-and-hold
questions.explain: Trend following earns its return in a handful of bars nobody can pick in advance. Selling on each scary pullback captures the chop and misses the move; the activity limit forces you to size a stop that survives normal pullbacks instead.

questions.q: In a trend drill, which action does the lesson call the one unforgivable act?
choices: Adding a small amount on a higher low
Trailing the stop up under a new swing low
Moving a stop down, away from price, as the trade goes against you
Letting the trend run without taking profit
questions.explain: A stop that moves away from price is a decision to take a bigger loss later. Trailing a stop up locks in gains; adding on a higher low is constructive. Lowering a stop undermines the only risk control that always works.

questions.q: Why does the SMA crossover drill require you to take every crossover, including the ones that follow three losers?
choices: Because taking every signal is the only way to learn the rule's real distribution of outcomes, and the one big winner that pays for the whipsaws often follows a cluster of losses
Because crossovers are always profitable in the long run
Because the engine will not let you skip a signal
Because skipping signals increases the win rate
questions.explain: Taken selectively, a rule is not a rule. Mechanical execution shows the pattern every backtest shows: several whipsaws, then a crossover that catches a long move. Skipping that one means the system worked and you did not.

questions.q: How does the breakout drill ask you to enter a position?
choices: With a market order as soon as the breakout is obvious
With a limit order below the base, hoping for a pullback
With a buy stop placed a little above the base's resistance, so the market pulls you in only if it breaks out
By shorting the resistance level
questions.explain: A buy stop above resistance removes the chase-or-wait dilemma: you are filled at roughly the breakout price while doing nothing, and never own the stock if it fails to break out. A sell stop under the base then protects the entry.

questions.q: What does a false breakout typically cost a trader using the buy-stop-above-resistance, sell-stop-under-base method?
choices: Nothing, because the buy stop never fills
Roughly the height of the base, as the buy stop fills above resistance and the sell stop fills under the base
The entire position, because there is no exit
Half of the account, because of leverage
questions.explain: The entry is just above the top of the base and the protective stop just below its bottom, so a failed breakout loses about the base's height plus slippage. Keeping those small while letting true breakouts run is the whole method.

questions.q: Which statistical shape does a mean-reversion method usually have, compared with trend following?
choices: Low win rate and large average winners
High win rate and small average winners, with occasional large losses when the stretch keeps stretching
Both win rate and average winner are higher than trend following
It has no losses because prices always revert
questions.explain: Prices usually snap back a little, so reversal trades win often; but you are selling into a move rather than riding one, so the wins are small, and the trade that does not revert is the start of a new trend and can erase many winners. That is why precise entries and hard stops matter more here.

questions.q: Why does the range-trading drill require at least two limit orders?
choices: Limit orders are the only orders the replay engine supports
The edge in a reversal trade is only a few percent, and chasing with market orders gives much of it away; a limit order gets your price or no trade
Limit orders always fill
Market orders are not allowed in ranging markets
questions.explain: A reversal trader's edge is buying a little lower and selling a little higher than the crowd. Limit orders near support and resistance capture that; if the market does not come to your price, there was no trade.

questions.q: In the crash drill with ticks on, a daily bar opens 8% below your resting sell stop. What happens, and what is the only fix that always works?
choices: The stop fills at the stop price; nothing needs fixing
The stop fills at the open, far below your stop price; the only reliable protection is position size
The stop is cancelled automatically; use a stop-limit instead
The stop fills at the previous close; use a wider stop
questions.explain: A gap skips the stop price, so the stop becomes a market order filled at the first available price, the open. Stop-limits avoid a bad fill but may leave you in. Sizing so that a gap twice your stop distance is still a small loss is the protection that always works.

questions.q: ATR roughly triples during a panic. What does the lesson say that implies for your stops and position sizes?
choices: Tighten stops and increase size, because the moves are bigger
Keep both the same; rules should never change
Widen stops with ATR so they sit outside the noise, and shrink size to match so the dollar risk stays constant
Remove stops entirely until the volatility passes
questions.explain: A stop that was a sensible 3% below price is inside a 10% daily range and fires on noise. Widening the stop with ATR keeps it meaningful, and shrinking size keeps the risk per trade at 1% of equity despite the wider stop.

questions.q: Why does the intraday drill cap you at four round trips and require you to be flat at the close?
choices: Because the engine only has four trades of data
Because overtrading to get back to even is the classic intraday failure, and an overnight gap on an intraday position is how small accounts end
Because day traders are not allowed to short
Because VWAP resets after four trades
questions.explain: The trade cap makes overtrading a fail rather than a feeling. Going home flat is the day trader's one inviolable rule: a position sized for a 2% intraday drawdown can lose many times that in an overnight gap.

questions.q: The bear-market survival drill does not require a positive return, only a drawdown under 15%, a result ahead of buy-and-hold, and at least one stop order. What is the lesson behind those criteria?
choices: That shorting is mandatory in a bear market
That cash is a legitimate position and survival, not prediction, is the goal; the stop requirement makes you take at least one well-sized trade
That buy-and-hold always wins
That drawdown does not matter if the year ends positive
questions.explain: You cannot know in advance which market you are in, so the question is how much you lose if wrong. Sitting mostly in cash passes the first two criteria; the stop requirement ensures you practise one protected position in a hostile market.

questions.q: You have $100,000 of equity and want to buy a $200 stock with a stop $16 below your entry. Under the 1% rule, how many shares do you buy?
choices: 500 shares, so the position is $100,000
100 shares, a round number
62 shares, because $1,000 of risk divided by $16 of stop distance is 62.5, rounded down
16 shares, one per dollar of stop distance
questions.explain: Risk budget is 1% of equity, $1,000. Divide by the stop distance of $16 per share and round down: 62 shares, a position of about $12,400. The share count is an output of the stop, never an input.

questions.q: Why does averaging down fail the bear-market drill's drawdown criterion so reliably?
choices: Because the engine forbids buying the same stock twice
Because it doubles your exposure to a falling position while improving only the story, converting a small loss into a large one
Because it increases commission
Because it only works for short positions
questions.explain: Buying more of a position that is down 40% lowers your average cost and doubles your exposure. In a continuing decline the loss grows faster than the improved average helps, and the drawdown limit catches it.

questions.q: In the short-selling drill, you try to short $250,000 of stock in a $100,000 account and the order is rejected. Why?
choices: Short selling is disabled in replay
The paper engine requires cash after the sale equal to 150% of the short's value, and $100,000 + $250,000 is less than $250,000 × 1.5
You can only short after a buy stop is placed
The stock is on a hard-to-borrow list
questions.explain: The margin rule from Module 4 is enforced by the engine: cash after the sale must equal at least 150% of the short's value. After the sale you would hold $350,000 in cash, but 150% of $250,000 is $375,000, so the order is rejected. The largest short the rule allows in a $100,000 account is $200,000 (cash + proceeds = 1.5 × short value). The rejection is doing your risk management for you; reduce the size until the rule is satisfied.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call position size the only risk control that works on every bar?
choices: Because stops never fail
Because indicators are always right at turning points
Because stops fail on gaps, indicators fail at turns and judgement fails under stress, while a small position caps the worst plausible loss regardless
Because the engine forces a maximum position size
questions.explain: Every other control depends on something cooperating: the market trading through your stop, the indicator being right, you staying calm. A position sized so the worst plausible outcome is a small percentage of equity needs none of that.

questions.q: Two replay sessions both return +12%. One made 3 trades with a 6% maximum drawdown; the other made 14 trades with a 15% drawdown. What does the lesson say about them?
choices: They are equally good; the return is the same
The 14-trade session is better because more trades means more practice
The 3-trade session is the better one: same return with less pain and less activity, which only the scorecard reveals
Neither counts unless the return beats 20%
