questions.explain: Return alone hides how a result was achieved. Smaller drawdown and fewer trades for the same return means more return per unit of risk and less activity that did not help. Comparing drawdown with return across all drills is the habit to build.

questions.q: A trend drill ends with a 40% win rate and a profit factor of 1.8. How should you read that?
choices: As a failure, because the win rate is below 50%
As the expected shape of a trend method: winners much larger than losers, which is what profit factor above 1 with a low win rate means
As a sign that the stop was too tight
As meaningless, because profit factor only matters for reversal trades
questions.explain: Win rate must be compared with the method, not with 50%. Trend following wins less often and wins bigger; a profit factor of 1.8 says gross profits were 1.8 times gross losses despite losing most trades.

questions.q: Which journal field does the lesson say to use for grading yourself, and on what basis?
choices: Return, on whether the session made money
Rating 1 to 5, on how well you followed the plan regardless of profit
Confidence, on how sure you felt
Win rate, against 50%
questions.explain: The replay account resets every session; only you carry over. Grading on rule-following produces the data for the two-column expectancy test and trains the one skill that transfers to a live account. A losing session with every rule followed is a 5.

questions.q: In the weekly review, sessions you rated 4 or 5 average −1% and sessions rated 1 to 3 average +3%. What does that mean?
choices: Your discipline is the problem; follow the rules more carefully
Your rules are wrong, so following them more carefully will not help; return to the backtester
You should trade only when you feel like breaking the rules
The journal has a bug
questions.explain: If following the plan loses and breaking it wins, the plan is the problem, not the discipline. That is a signal to revisit the method's rules in the strategy lab, not to try harder at obeying rules that lose.

questions.q: Why is 'don't trade in May' a bad rule change for repeating a demo drill, while 'use a 2 × ATR stop instead of a fixed 3%' is a good one?
choices: Because May is always a profitable month
Because the first fits the bars you now remember from the first run (look-ahead bias), while the second would apply on any chart and is a genuine experiment
Because the engine does not allow date-based rules
Because ATR stops always make more money
questions.explain: Demo bars are deterministic, so a repeat is only an honest experiment if the changed rule is one you could apply to a chart you have never seen. A rule that happens to fit the remembered bars is hindsight dressed as a rule, the same disease as look-ahead bias in backtests.

questions.q: Which of these is a process goal rather than an outcome goal?
choices: Make 15% this year
Every trade has a stop order placed at the same time as the entry
Double the account in 18 months
Beat the S&P 500 by five percentage points
questions.explain: A process goal is something you fully control and can score as a percentage of trades. The other three depend on what the market does, which no plan can guarantee.

questions.q: A student can look at charts only after 5 pm on weekdays and for an hour on Sunday. Which timeframe does that constraint point to?
choices: 5-minute bars with trades during the open
Hourly bars managed through the session
Daily bars with orders placed in the evening and checked once a day
It makes no difference; any timeframe can be traded from a phone
questions.explain: If you cannot watch the regular session, intraday rules cannot be executed as written. Daily bars with resting limit and stop orders fit the schedule.

questions.q: How should the plan's maximum drawdown limit be chosen?
choices: Pick the deepest drawdown you have actually tolerated calmly in paper or replay, or less
Use the index's historical worst drawdown
Pick a round number that sounds disciplined, such as 50%
There should be no limit; drawdowns are part of trading
questions.explain: Tolerance is a fact about you, measured from how you behaved in past drawdowns. If the rules produce deeper drawdowns than that in testing, the rules change, not the limit.

questions.q: Your real trading capital will be $3,000 but your paper account is $100,000. What does the lesson recommend?
choices: Keep $100,000 so the statistics are smoother
Reset the paper account to $3,000 with a realistic commission so habits form at true scale
Trade the paper account at 30 times normal size to compensate
Switch to options, which need less capital
questions.explain: Position-sizing habits only transfer if the paper account is the size of the real one. A 1% risk on $3,000 is $30, and learning what that buys is part of the plan.

questions.q: What is the point of the "Where I start from" self-audit paragraph?
choices: To impress a future employer
To record the baseline (adherence, best and worst setups, when rules get broken) that later reviews are compared against
To estimate next year's return
To decide which indicator is the most accurate
questions.explain: The audit forces the plan to be written for the trader you actually are, and it gives the quarterly review in Lesson 5 something concrete to measure progress against.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend liquid US stocks and index ETFs as the default instruments for a first trading plan?
choices: They always go up
Costs are tiny, there is no expiry, and the app's engines model them best
Regulators require beginners to trade them
They are the only instruments with charts
questions.explain: Narrow spreads and no commission keep the cost hurdle low, no expiry means an early thesis is not automatically a loss, and the paper, replay and backtest engines were built around them.

questions.q: Six of the eight names in a watchlist are semiconductor stocks with pairwise correlations near 0.9. What is the problem?
choices: The watchlist is too small
They are effectively one position; a sector move hits all six at once, so diversification is an illusion
Semiconductors cannot be charted
Correlation only matters for options
questions.explain: Highly correlated names move together. Six positions in them carry roughly the risk of one large position, which breaks the per-trade and total-heat limits in spirit. Cap positions per sector or thin the list.

questions.q: What does "trade on one timeframe, filter on the one above it" mean in practice?
choices: Use two charts of the same interval
Take entries from the trading timeframe only when the higher timeframe's trend agrees, for example daily breakouts only when the 200-day slope is up
Switch to a lower timeframe when a stop is near
Average the two timeframes' prices
questions.explain: The higher timeframe defines the trend; the lower one times the entry. The filter removes many whipsaws in ranges and is easy to test in the lab by comparing with and without it.

questions.q: Under what condition does the lesson allow options in the plan?
choices: Whenever a stock is too expensive to buy 100 shares
Never
Only defined-risk forms in a separate section with their own rules, including maximum premium per trade and a minimum days-to-expiry rule
Only naked short options, which have the highest win rate
questions.explain: Long calls and puts, vertical spreads, covered calls and protective puts have known maximum losses. The plan must state why an option beats the stock for a specific setup and how it is sized; otherwise the setup is a stock trade.

questions.q: Why write three comparison symbols outside the universe into the plan?
choices: To have more charts to look at
So every new rule is tested on names you did not pick for their convenience, guarding against curve-fitting to the watchlist
Because the backtest engine requires at least four symbols
To diversify the paper account
questions.explain: A rule that only works on the names you chose may have found stories about those stocks. Pre-committing to outside test symbols makes the out-of-sample check honest.

questions.q: Which of these entry rules passes the "stranger test"?
choices: Buy when momentum is clearly picking up
Buy when the chart looks like it is about to break out
Buy at the next open when yesterday's close is above the 20-day SMA, the 50-day SMA is above the 200-day SMA, and yesterday's close is the highest close of the last 20 days
Buy when you feel confident about the company
questions.explain: A rule passes when two readers would act identically on the same chart. Only the third option consists entirely of checkable comparisons between numbers.

questions.q: Your equity is $20,000, risk per trade is 1%, entry is $50 and the initial stop is $46. How many shares does the plan's formula give?
questions.explain: Shares = (equity x risk%) / (entry minus stop) = ($20,000 x 0.01) / ($50 - $46) = $200 / $4 = 50 shares. The position is worth $2,500 but the amount at risk is $200.

questions.q: Your plan has a 10-bar time stop. A swing trade is now 10 bars old, sitting a few cents above entry, and neither the stop nor the target has been touched. What does the plan say to do?
choices: Hold on: a trade that has not lost money is still working
Close it now and free the capital; a trade that has gone nowhere in its allotted time has failed the setup even though it never hit the stop
Move the stop to breakeven and give it ten more bars
Add to the position to speed things up
questions.explain: The time stop is an exit rule, not a suggestion. Capital parked in a stale trade cannot take the next live signal, and journals show dead trades often decay into losses. Extending the deadline because the trade 'has not lost yet' is exactly the discretionary drift the plan exists to prevent; if ten bars is wrong for your setup, change the rule at the quarterly review, not mid-trade.

questions.q: The plan says total heat is capped at 5% of equity. You have four open positions each risking 1.25%, and a valid signal fires. What do you do?
choices: Take it at half size
Take it and tighten the other stops
Skip it and log it as a skipped signal with the reason
Close the weakest position to make room
questions.explain: When the cap is reached, no new entries, even valid ones. Logging the skip keeps the record honest and lets the review judge whether the cap is set correctly.

questions.q: When may the plan's rules be changed?
choices: Immediately after a loss, while the lesson is fresh
Whenever a trade is going badly
Only at the scheduled review, one change at a time, with the reason and evidence written down
Never; a plan is permanent
questions.explain: Changes made after a loss are revenge in disguise and changes after a win are overconfidence. The review is the only time the plan is editable; between reviews it is read-only.

questions.q: Why are the pass criteria for each validation gate written down before the test is run?
choices: Because the lab requires them as inputs
So the result is judged against a standard set in advance rather than one chosen to fit the outcome
To save time
Because criteria cannot be changed later under any circumstances
questions.explain: A result judged against criteria chosen afterwards is a story, not a test. Criteria can change, but only at the scheduled review with the reason recorded.

questions.q: A rule shows a profit factor of 2.1 with a 20-day lookback, but 0.8 at 18 days and 0.9 at 22 days. What does this suggest?
choices: The rule is robust and 20 is the optimal setting
The result at 20 is probably noise; a sound rule shows a broad plateau across neighbouring parameter values
The data must be wrong
The rule needs a longer backtest
questions.explain: Sensitivity to a single parameter value is a hallmark of curve-fitting. The optimizer grid should show a plateau; a sharp peak means the parameter found the past, not an edge.

questions.q: What does the replay gate test that the backtest gate does not?
choices: Whether the rule is profitable
Whether you can execute the rule bar by bar with the future hidden, without breaking it
Whether the data provider is accurate
Whether the rule works on intraday bars
questions.explain: The backtest tests the rule; replay tests the trader applying the rule under uncertainty. Adherence, not profit, is the main pass criterion for the replay gate.

questions.q: What can thirty paper trades realistically prove?
choices: That the strategy has a statistically significant edge
That you can follow written rules for months, and whether there are gross execution problems the backtest hid
That the strategy will work with real money
Nothing; only backtests matter
questions.explain: With a 50% win rate the 95% range for the win rate over 30 trades is roughly 32% to 68%, so an edge cannot be confirmed. Adherence and execution problems can be, and that is the point of the gate.

questions.q: Gate 3 ends with 94% adherence but a slightly negative expectancy after costs. What does the lesson recommend?
choices: Abandon trading
Go live anyway because adherence was high
Return to gate 1, make exactly one change to the rules with its reason recorded, and re-test
Make several changes at once to fix it faster
questions.explain: High adherence means the method, not the behaviour, needs work, so the fix belongs in the backtest gate. One change at a time keeps cause and effect visible.

questions.q: A stock is quoted bid $84.20, ask $84.26. You buy 200 shares with a market order and sell them immediately with another market order. Ignoring commissions, what is your result?
choices: Break even
A loss of $12, the spread on 200 shares
A gain of $12
A loss of $0.06
questions.explain: You buy at the ask ($84.26) and sell at the bid ($84.20), losing $0.06 per share x 200 = $12. The spread is a cost paid on every round trip before price moves at all.

questions.q: On a daily chart a stock makes a series of higher highs and higher lows above a rising 50-day moving average. Which description fits?
choices: A downtrend
A range
An uptrend; a trend-following plan looks for pullback entries, a mean-reversion plan stays out
A head-and-shoulders top
questions.explain: Higher highs and higher lows with a rising average define an uptrend. Mean-reversion entries against a strong trend are exactly the trades the lesson warned against.

questions.q: RSI(14) on a stock drops to 22 while the stock is in a steep, persistent downtrend below a falling 200-day average. What is the correct reading for a plan that uses an RSI mean-reversion setup?
choices: Buy immediately; oversold always bounces
Oversold can stay oversold in a trend; the setup requires a ranging stock, so no trade
Short the stock because RSI is low
RSI is irrelevant on daily charts
questions.explain: Oscillators measure momentum, not value. In a strong downtrend RSI can stay below 30 for weeks. The setup conditions, not the trigger alone, decide whether a signal is valid.

questions.q: Your account equity is $12,000, risk per trade is 1%, entry $36.00, stop $34.50. Position size?
choices: 333 shares
80 shares
120 shares
8 shares
questions.explain: Risk = $120. Distance to stop = $1.50. Shares = $120 / $1.50 = 80. Position value is $2,880, but only $120 is at risk if the stop is honoured.

questions.q: A strategy wins 40% of the time with an average winner of 2.5R and an average loser of 1.0R. What is its expectancy per trade, and is it a good sign?
choices: -0.1R; it loses
+0.4R; positive, so the method can be profitable despite losing most trades
+1.5R; exceptional
Cannot be computed without the win count
questions.explain: Expectancy = 0.4 x 2.5 - 0.6 x 1.0 = 1.0 - 0.6 = +0.4R per trade. A sub-50% win rate with large winners is typical of a healthy trend-following plan.

questions.q: A stock trades at $100. You buy one $105 call expiring in 30 days for $2.00. At expiry the stock is $104. What is your result?
choices: A gain of $200
A loss of $200, the whole premium
A loss of $100
Break even
questions.explain: The call is out of the money at expiry ($104 is below the $105 strike), so it expires worthless and the entire $2.00 x 100 = $200 premium is lost. That is the defined maximum loss of a long call.

questions.q: A backtest of a rule returns 60% a year, but the strategy uses the day's close to decide whether to buy at that same day's open. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; it is a good result
Look-ahead bias: the rule uses information unavailable at the time of the decision, so the result is meaningless
Survivorship bias
The return is too low to be interesting
questions.explain: Any rule that uses data from after the moment of the decision is cheating. Honest rules act on the next bar's open using only completed bars. The lab's built-ins are written this way.

questions.q: In a replay session you are long, price is approaching your stop, and you switch the chart to the 15-minute interval to "see what it is really doing". According to your plan, what has just happened?
choices: Good risk management
A rule break: changing timeframe during a trade, usually to find a reason not to take the stop
A valid higher-timeframe filter
Nothing, since replay is practice
questions.explain: The plan forbids changing timeframe mid-trade in one sentence because it is one of the most common ways stops get rationalized away. Replay exists to catch this habit before money is involved.

questions.q: After 30 paper trades your adherence is 72% and the followed-plan column has positive expectancy while the broken-plan column is strongly negative. What does this tell you and what is the next step?
choices: The method is broken; redesign the rules
The method works and discipline is the problem; the next 30 trades stay on paper with a behavioural fix, such as smaller size or a pre-trade checklist
Go live immediately since the followed trades were profitable
Add a second setup to diversify
questions.explain: The two-column test separates method from behaviour. Positive when followed and negative when broken means the rules are fine and you are not following them; that is fixed behaviourally, not by editing rules.

questions.q: When, according to the plan, may you edit the rules?
choices: Whenever a trade goes badly
Daily, after the close
Only at the scheduled quarterly review, one change at a time, with evidence recorded and the backtest gate re-run before adoption
Only after a losing streak of five
questions.explain: Weekly reviews change behaviour, monthly reviews adjust risk by the scaling rule, and only the quarterly review may change a rule. Each change is one at a time, written down, and re-tested through gate 1 first.

questions.q: A stock is quoted 48.20 bid / 48.26 ask. You place a market order to buy 100 shares. Roughly what do you pay?
choices: $4,823, the midpoint
Whatever the last trade printed
questions.explain: A market buy takes the ask. 100 x $48.26 = $4,826. The bid is what you would receive if you sold.

questions.q: Stock A is quoted 20.00 / 20.02 and stock B is quoted 20.00 / 20.40. Which is the better statement?
choices: A is less liquid than B
B costs 2% of its price just to buy and immediately sell
The spread does not matter if you hold for a month
B is a better trade because the ask is higher
questions.explain: B's spread is $0.40 on a $20 stock: 2%. Buying at the ask and selling at the bid loses that instantly. A's spread is 0.1%. Wide spreads are a sign of poor liquidity.

questions.q: You own shares bought at $60 and set a stop order at $55. Overnight the company reports bad news and the stock opens at $47. What happens?
choices: Your shares are sold at $55
Nothing; stops only work during the day they are placed
The stop triggers at the open and sells at about $47
The broker cancels the order because the gap is too large
questions.explain: A stop becomes a market order when the price touches or passes the stop level. The first price available after a gap down is around $47, so that is where it fills. A stop limits loss, but not through gaps.

questions.q: You want to buy a stock trading at $100 only if it breaks out above $105. Which order type does this?
choices: A limit buy at $105
A buy stop at $105
A market order placed now
A sell stop at $105
questions.explain: A buy stop sits above the market and becomes a market buy when the price reaches $105. A limit buy at $105 would fill immediately, because $105 is above the current price.

questions.q: What is the main risk of a limit order compared with a market order?
choices: It may fill at a worse price than expected
It may never fill
It costs a higher commission
It can only be used for buying
questions.explain: A limit order guarantees the price but not the fill. If the market never trades at your limit, the order stays open and you miss the move.

questions.q: Regular US stock market hours are:
choices: 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. New York time
9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. New York time
9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. New York time
24 hours on weekdays
questions.explain: The NYSE and Nasdaq regular session is 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. New York time, Monday to Friday, excluding exchange holidays. Pre- and after-hours sessions exist but are thin.

questions.q: A company earns $4.00 per share and its stock trades at $80. Its P/E ratio is:
questions.explain: P/E is price divided by earnings per share: $80 / $4 = 20. You are paying 20 years of current profit for each share.

questions.q: Which of these is the best description of paper trading?
choices: Trading only paper and packaging company stocks
Trading with simulated money to practise without risk
Trading by filling out paper order tickets
A strategy that only buys on paper record highs
questions.explain: Paper trading means simulated trading: real or demo prices, pretend money. It teaches mechanics and discipline without the cost of mistakes, though it cannot fully reproduce the emotions of real losses.

questions.q: A company has 50 million shares outstanding, of which insiders hold 30 million that they rarely trade. A trader says it has a "small float". What does that mean for price behaviour?
choices: Dividends will be smaller
The stock cannot be shorted
Fewer shares are available to trade, so moderate volume can move the price a lot
The market cap is calculated on 20 million shares
questions.explain: The float is the 20 million shares actually available to trade. Market cap still uses all 50 million shares. A small float means relatively small buying or selling can move the price sharply.

questions.q: Which statement about the demo data in Broward Trading is correct?
choices: It is delayed real market data
It is a simulated, deterministic price series that is the same for every student
It is live data from the NYSE
It is random and different every time you reload
questions.explain: Demo mode is a seeded random walk per symbol. It is not real market data, which is why the dashboard shows a DEMO pill, and it is deterministic so that drills and lessons refer to the same bars for everyone.

questions.q: A daily candle has open 100, high 104, low 97 and close 98. Which is true?
choices: The body is green (bullish) and spans 97 to 104
The body is red (bearish) and spans 98 to 100
The body spans 97 to 104 and the colour depends on yesterday
There is no body because the high is above the open
questions.explain: The body runs from the open to the close: 100 down to 98, so it is red (the close is below the open). The wicks reach the high of 104 and the low of 97.

questions.q: A stock is in a strong uptrend on the daily chart but a sharp downtrend on the 5-minute chart. For a trader who holds for several weeks, which matters more?
choices: The 5-minute chart, because it is the most recent information
The daily chart, because it matches the holding period
Neither; only the weekly chart matters
Both equally
questions.explain: Match the timeframe to the holding period. Intraday wiggles are noise to a swing trader; the daily trend is the tide they are swimming in. The 5-minute chart may help time the entry, nothing more.

questions.q: A stock has bounced from $48-$49 three times. It now closes at $46.50 on heavy volume. What is the most reasonable reading?
choices: Support held again
Support has broken; $48-$49 may now act as resistance
This is a buying opportunity because the stock is cheaper
Volume is irrelevant to support levels
questions.explain: A decisive close through a tested support zone, confirmed by volume, is a breakdown. Broken support often becomes resistance as trapped buyers sell into any rally back to their entry.

questions.q: Which sequence describes an uptrend?
choices: Lower highs and lower lows
Higher highs and higher lows
Equal highs and equal lows
Higher highs and lower lows
questions.explain: An uptrend is defined by swing highs that exceed previous highs and swing lows that stay above previous lows. The first lower low is an early warning that the trend may be changing.

questions.q: A stock breaks above resistance at $55 on volume that is 40% of its daily average. How should a careful trader read this?
choices: A confirmed breakout; buy immediately
A suspect breakout; low volume means few participants agree, so it may fail
Low volume breakouts are more reliable
Volume only matters for breakdowns
questions.explain: Volume confirmation is the principle that a move on heavy volume reflects broad agreement. A breakout on thin volume is easier to reverse and is a classic false-breakout setup.

questions.q: After a two-week decline, a stock opens at 45, trades down to 42, and closes at 44.80. What pattern is this and what does it suggest?
choices: A shooting star; bearish
A hammer; sellers pushed price down but buyers took it back, a possible bottom
A doji; indecision
A bearish engulfing candle
questions.explain: A small body near the top with a long lower wick after a decline is a hammer. It shows rejection of lower prices. Confirmation comes from a higher close on the next bar.

questions.q: Day 1: open 60, close 61. Day 2: open 61.40, close 58.70. Day 2 is best described as:
choices: A bullish engulfing candle
A bearish engulfing candle
A morning star
An inside bar
questions.explain: Day 2's red body (61.40 down to 58.70) completely covers Day 1's green body (60 to 61). After a rally, that is a bearish engulfing pattern: sellers overwhelmed buyers.

questions.q: A doji candle mainly tells you:
choices: The trend will definitely reverse
Buyers and sellers ended the period roughly where they started: indecision
Volume was very high
The stock will gap tomorrow
questions.explain: A doji has almost no body because the open and close are nearly equal. It signals indecision; after a strong run it hints that the trend may be pausing, but it needs confirmation.

questions.q: A head and shoulders pattern has a head at $64, shoulders near $58 and $57, and a neckline at $52. Price closes at $51. The classic measured target is about:
questions.explain: The measured move projects the head-to-neckline height (64 - 52 = 12) below the neckline: 52 - 12 = 40. Targets are estimates, not guarantees; manage the trade with a stop above the right shoulder.

questions.q: Which pattern is a continuation pattern rather than a reversal pattern?
choices: Head and shoulders
Double top
Bull flag
Evening star
questions.explain: A flag is a brief pause after a sharp move that usually resolves in the direction of the move. Head and shoulders, double tops and evening stars are reversal patterns.

questions.q: A stock breaks out above $55, then two days later dips to $55.20 and bounces. This is called a:
choices: False breakout
Retest of the breakout level
Breakdown
Death cross
questions.explain: A retest is when price returns to a broken level and holds. Old resistance acting as new support confirms the breakout and offers a lower-risk entry with a stop just below $55.

questions.q: The last five closes are 20, 22, 24, 26 and 28. The 5-period SMA is:
questions.explain: The SMA is the plain average: (20 + 22 + 24 + 26 + 28) / 5 = 24. Note how the average lags the current price (28) in a trend.

questions.q: Compared with a 20-period SMA, a 20-period EMA will:
choices: Lag more, because it is exponential
React faster to recent prices but whipsaw more
Always sit above the SMA
Give identical values
questions.explain: The EMA weights recent closes more heavily, so it turns sooner than the SMA of the same length. The cost of speed is more false signals in choppy markets.

questions.q: A golden cross occurs when:
choices: Price crosses above the 200-day SMA
The 50-day SMA crosses above the 200-day SMA
RSI crosses above 50
The 200-day SMA crosses above the 50-day SMA
questions.explain: The golden cross is the 50-day SMA rising through the 200-day SMA. It is a lagging confirmation of a long-term uptrend, usually printing well after the low.

questions.q: Over the last 14 days a stock's average gain is 1.5 and its average loss is 0.5. Its RSI is approximately:
questions.explain: RS = 1.5 / 0.5 = 3. RSI = 100 - 100 / (1 + 3) = 75. A reading above 70 is called overbought, although strong trends can hold it there.

questions.q: A stock makes a new high at $65 (previous high $60) while RSI peaks at 68 (previous peak 76). This is:
choices: Bullish divergence; momentum is accelerating
Bearish divergence; price rose but momentum did not confirm
A golden cross
Nothing unusual; RSI always falls as price rises
questions.explain: Higher price high with a lower RSI high is bearish divergence. It warns that the rally is losing momentum and often precedes a pullback. It is a warning, not a sell signal on its own.

questions.q: The stochastic oscillator's %K is 80. What does that say about the latest close?
choices: It is 80% of the all-time high
It is 80% of the way up the recent high-low range
RSI must also be 80
Volume is 80% above average
questions.explain: Stochastic %K places the close within the lookback range: (close - lowest low) / (highest high - lowest low) x 100. A reading of 80 means the close is near the top of the range.

questions.q: The MACD line is 1.2 and the signal line is 1.0. The histogram is:
questions.explain: The histogram is MACD minus signal: 1.2 - 1.0 = +0.2. Positive and growing bars mean bullish momentum is building; shrinking bars warn it is fading before any crossover.

questions.q: A 20-day SMA is at 50 and the 20-day standard deviation of closes is 2. With the standard setting, the Bollinger Bands are at:
choices: 48 and 52
46 and 54
40 and 60
49 and 51
questions.explain: Standard Bollinger Bands sit two standard deviations from the middle band: 50 - 4 = 46 and 50 + 4 = 54. Roughly 90-95% of closes fall inside.

questions.q: A stock has a 14-day ATR of $2.00. You buy at $80 and want a stop 2 ATR away. Where is the stop?
questions.explain: Two ATR is $4, so the stop sits at $80 - $4 = $76. ATR-based stops adapt to each stock's volatility instead of using an arbitrary dollar amount.

questions.q: When Bollinger Bands narrow to their tightest level in months, this "squeeze" usually means:
choices: The stock will rise
The stock will fall
Volatility is low and a larger move often follows, direction unknown
The indicator is broken
questions.explain: A squeeze marks low volatility. Volatility is cyclical, so squeezes often precede expansions, but the bands do not say which way. Wait for the breakout and confirm it with volume.

questions.q: ADX is 14. +DI just crossed above -DI. What is the sound interpretation?
choices: A strong buy signal
A weak signal: ADX below 20 says there is no meaningful trend to follow
A sell signal
ADX of 14 means a 14% uptrend
questions.explain: ADX measures trend strength regardless of direction. Below 20 the market is ranging and DI crossovers whipsaw. The crossover becomes meaningful when ADX rises above 20-25.

questions.q: Today 1,000 shares traded at $50 and 3,000 shares traded at $52. VWAP is:
questions.explain: VWAP weights each price by its volume: (50 x 1,000 + 52 x 3,000) / 4,000 = 206,000 / 4,000 = $51.50.

questions.q: Price has moved sideways for two weeks while OBV has risen steadily. This suggests:
choices: Distribution: sellers are quietly unloading
Accumulation: volume is heavier on up days, hinting at buying under the surface
OBV is broken because price is flat
A guaranteed breakout tomorrow
questions.explain: OBV adds volume on up closes and subtracts it on down closes. Rising OBV with flat price means more volume on up days: accumulation. It raises the odds of an upside breakout but promises nothing.

questions.q: A stock rallied from $40 to $50. The 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level is at about:
questions.explain: Retracements measure how far price gives back the move: 50 - 0.618 x (50 - 40) = 50 - 6.18 = $43.82. The 50% level would be $45.

questions.q: Which pair correctly labels a lagging and a leading indicator?
choices: Lagging: RSI divergence; Leading: 200-day SMA
Lagging: 200-day SMA; Leading: RSI divergence
Both are leading
Both are lagging
questions.explain: Moving averages are built from past prices and confirm trends after they start (lagging). Oscillator divergences try to warn before a turn (leading), at the cost of more false alarms.

questions.q: The dashboard shows BUY with a score of 5 out of 8, listing reasons like "price above SMA50" and "MACD above signal". What is the right way to use this?
choices: Buy immediately; the computer has decided
Read the reasons, check them against the chart and your plan, and use the score as context, not a command
Ignore it; composite signals are always wrong
Wait for 8 out of 8 before any trade
questions.explain: The composite signal exists to show its reasoning. It is a structured summary of several indicators, not a prediction. Your rules, risk and timeframe still decide the trade.

questions.q: A 20/50 SMA cross system produced five signals in six weeks, each reversing within days, while price stayed between $50 and $55. This behaviour is called:
choices: A squeeze
Divergence
Whipsaw
Golden cross
questions.explain: Whipsaws are rapid false signals in a sideways market. Trend-following rules whipsaw in ranges by design; filters such as ADX > 25 or accepting the small losses are the usual responses.

questions.q: You have a $50,000 account and risk 1% per trade. You buy a stock at $40 with a stop at $37. How many shares?
questions.explain: Risk budget: 1% of $50,000 = $500. Risk per share: $40 - $37 = $3. Shares = 500 / 3 = 166 (round down). The position is $6,640, far more than $500, but only $500 is at risk if the stop holds.

questions.q: According to the 1% rule, the amount you should risk on one trade with a $100,000 account is about:
questions.explain: One percent of $100,000 is $1,000: the loss if the stop is hit, not the size of the position. Ten losses in a row would cost about 10% of the account, which is survivable.

questions.q: Two stocks: A has an ATR of $1 and B has an ATR of $4, both priced at $100. With the same dollar risk and a 2-ATR stop, which position holds more shares?
choices: A, four times as many
B, four times as many
They are equal because the prices are equal
Cannot tell without the win rate
questions.explain: A's stop is $2 away, B's is $8 away. For the same dollar risk, A gets four times as many shares. Position size should shrink as volatility rises.

questions.q: Entry $50, stop $47, target $56. The risk/reward ratio is:
questions.explain: Risk is $3 (50 - 47), reward is $6 (56 - 50). Reward divided by risk is 2, a 2:1 ratio. At 2:1 you can be right only 40% of the time and still profit.

questions.q: A strategy wins 35% of the time. Winners average $400 and losers average $150. Its expectancy per trade is:
questions.explain: Expectancy = 0.35 x 400 - 0.65 x 150 = 140 - 97.50 = +$42.50 per trade. A win rate under 50% is fine when winners are large relative to losers.

questions.q: Where does a stop-loss belong?
choices: At a round number like $5 below entry so it is easy to remember
Where the trade idea is proven wrong, such as just below the support you bought
As close as possible to the entry to keep losses tiny
Nowhere; stops just get you taken out
questions.explain: The stop goes where the setup is invalidated. Then position size is set from that distance. Stops placed by affordability or by habit are unrelated to the chart and get hit by noise.

questions.q: An account grows from $100,000 to $125,000, falls to $100,000, then recovers. The maximum drawdown was:
questions.explain: Drawdown is measured from the peak: (125,000 - 100,000) / 125,000 = 20%. Recovering from it needed a 25% gain, which is why drawdowns are asymmetric.

questions.q: A strategy wins 40% of the time. The probability of five losses in a row on any given five trades is about:
questions.explain: Each loss has probability 0.6, so five in a row is 0.6^5 = 0.078, about 8%. Over hundreds of trades such streaks are certain to appear. Sizing must survive them.

questions.q: Right after a losing trade, a trader doubles their size on an unplanned setup to "get it back". This is called:
choices: Hedging
Scaling in
Revenge trading
Mean reversion
questions.explain: Revenge trading is an emotional, oversized trade taken to recover a loss. It is the fastest way to turn a normal loss into a serious one, which is why trading plans include a daily loss limit.

questions.q: A trader holds a stock down 15% "until it gets back to my price" but sold a different winner at +3% because they were nervous. This pattern is best explained by:
choices: Good risk management
Loss aversion: losses feel heavier than gains, so losers are held and winners cut
Confirmation bias only
A high Sharpe ratio
questions.explain: Loss aversion makes a loss feel roughly twice as strong as an equal gain, leading to exactly this behaviour. It is the opposite of what positive expectancy requires: cut losers, let winners run.

questions.q: You short 100 shares at $50. The stock rises to $75 and you cover. Your result is:
questions.explain: Short profit is (sale price - buyback price) x shares = (50 - 75) x 100 = -$2,500. Short losses are unlimited in theory because there is no ceiling on the price.

questions.q: You buy $20,000 of stock using $10,000 of your own cash and $10,000 of margin. The stock falls 25%. Your loss on your own money is:
choices: 0%, the broker absorbs it
questions.explain: The position loses $5,000 (25% of $20,000), all of which comes out of your $10,000 equity: a 50% loss. Leverage doubles the gain and the loss, plus interest.

questions.q: A heavily shorted small-float stock jumps 20% on news and then closes up 80%. The extra move is most likely a:
choices: Dividend adjustment
Short squeeze: shorts forced to buy back, pushing the price higher
Golden cross
Stop-limit cascade
questions.explain: When a heavily shorted stock rises, short sellers face mounting losses and margin calls and must buy to cover. Their buying pushes the price higher, forcing more covering: a short squeeze.

questions.q: Which item does NOT belong in a trading plan?
choices: Exact entry and exit rules
Maximum risk per trade and per day
A list of stocks a friend said will go up
When and how you review your journal
questions.explain: A plan contains your rules, your risk limits and your review process. Tips from others are not rules you can test or repeat, and acting on them makes your results impossible to evaluate.

questions.q: The main purpose of a trading journal is to:
choices: Prove to others how good you are
Record setups, emotions and outcomes so you can find which behaviours make and lose money
Replace a trading plan
Calculate taxes
questions.explain: A journal turns anecdotes into data. Reviewing it reveals, for example, that your rule-breaking trades lose and your planned pullback entries win. Without it, you repeat the same mistakes.

questions.q: You own 100 shares bought at $50 and the stock trades at $47. Your position shows:
choices: A realized loss of $300
An unrealized loss of $300
No loss, because you have not sold
A realized gain of $300
questions.explain: Mark-to-market values the position at the current $47, an unrealized loss of $300. It becomes realized when you sell. "It is not a loss until I sell" is loss aversion talking; the account is already worth less.

questions.q: You buy a $50 call for a $2.00 premium. The stock closes at $55 at expiration. Ignoring commissions, your profit per contract is:
questions.explain: Intrinsic value at expiry is $55 - $50 = $5 per share. Minus the $2 premium leaves $3 per share, times the 100-share multiplier: $300 per contract.

questions.q: Buying a put option gives you:
choices: The obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike
The right to sell 100 shares at the strike before expiry
The right to buy 100 shares at the strike
A dividend from the company
questions.explain: A put is the right, not the obligation, to sell 100 shares at the strike before expiration. Puts gain value when the stock falls, making them insurance for shareholders.

questions.q: The stock is $52. A $50 call is priced at $3.20. How much of that premium is extrinsic (time) value?
questions.explain: Intrinsic value is stock minus strike: $52 - $50 = $2.00. The rest of the premium, $3.20 - $2.00 = $1.20, is extrinsic value: payment for time and volatility, which decays to zero at expiry.

questions.q: With the stock at $100, which option is out of the money?
choices: A $90 call
A $110 put
A $110 call
A $100 call
questions.explain: A call is out of the money when its strike is above the stock price. The $90 call and $110 put are in the money; the $100 call is at the money.

questions.q: A $100 call is quoted 3.10 / 3.30 with open interest of 12 contracts. Another strike is quoted 3.10 / 3.14 with open interest of 5,000. Which is the better statement?
choices: The first is more liquid because the spread is wider
The second is more liquid: tighter spread and far more open interest
Open interest does not affect your fills
Both cost the same to trade
questions.explain: A $0.20 spread on a $3.20 option costs over 6% to get in and out; $0.04 costs about 1%. High open interest means an active contract you can exit at a fair price.

questions.q: A call has a delta of 0.40. If the stock rises $1 (all else equal), the option price rises by about:
questions.explain: Delta is the option's sensitivity to a $1 move in the stock: about $0.40 per share, or $40 per contract. A 0.40 delta also suggests roughly a 40% chance of finishing in the money.

questions.q: An option has a theta of -0.05. If the stock price and volatility do not change, over one day the option loses about:
choices: $0.05 per contract
$5 per contract
$50 per contract
Nothing until expiry
questions.explain: Theta is quoted per share per day: $0.05 x 100 shares = $5 per contract per day. Time decay accelerates in the final weeks before expiration.

questions.q: A stock's options imply 45% volatility the day before earnings. The stock has historically moved about 25% annualised. After earnings, with the stock almost unchanged, a long straddle loses a lot of value. Why?
choices: Theta over one night is huge
Implied volatility collapsed after the event ("IV crush"), and long options have positive vega
Delta went to zero
The multiplier changed
questions.explain: Before a known event, IV is inflated to price the expected jump. Once the news is out, uncertainty and IV collapse. Long options (positive vega) lose value even if the stock barely moves.

questions.q: Gamma is highest for options that are:
choices: Deep in the money with a year to expiry
At the money and close to expiry
Far out of the money with a year to expiry
Any put option
questions.explain: Gamma measures how fast delta changes. Near expiry an at-the-money option flips between "worthless" and "like stock" with small price moves, so its delta swings fastest.

questions.q: You own 100 shares at $50 and sell a $55 call for $1.50. At expiry the stock is $60. Your outcome is:
choices: You keep the shares and the $150 premium
Shares are called away at $55; you made $5 per share plus the $1.50 premium, but gave up the move above $55
You lose $350
The call expires worthless
questions.explain: A covered call caps your gain at the strike. You sell at $55 (a $500 gain) and keep the $150 premium, $650 total, but forgo the extra $500 the shares earned above $55.

questions.q: Buy the $50 call for $3 and sell the $55 call for $1, same expiry. Maximum profit per share and breakeven are:
choices: Max profit $3, breakeven $52
Max profit $5, breakeven $53
Unlimited, breakeven $53
Max profit $2, breakeven $55
questions.explain: Net debit is $2. Max profit is the strike width minus the debit: $5 - $2 = $3 (if the stock is above $55 at expiry). Breakeven is the lower strike plus the debit: $52.

questions.q: Which position has defined (limited) risk?
choices: Short 100 shares of stock
A naked short call
A long put
A naked short put
questions.explain: A long option can lose at most the premium paid. Short stock and naked short calls have unlimited risk; a naked short put risks the full strike value if the stock goes to zero.

questions.q: Stock at $100. You buy the $100 call for $4 and the $100 put for $4. At expiry the position is profitable if the stock is:
choices: Anywhere between $96 and $104
Below $92 or above $108
Exactly $100
Above $104 only
questions.explain: A long straddle costs $8. It needs a move bigger than the premium in either direction: breakevens at $100 - $8 = $92 and $100 + $8 = $108.

questions.q: Stock at $100. You sell the $90 put and $110 call and buy the $85 put and $115 call for a net credit of $1.50. Your maximum loss per share is:
choices: Unlimited
questions.explain: This is an iron condor. Each wing is $5 wide. Max loss = wing width - credit = $5.00 - $1.50 = $3.50 per share ($350 per contract). Max profit is the $1.50 credit if the stock stays between $90 and $110.

questions.q: You sold a $100 put. The stock falls to $92 and the buyer exercises. What happens to you?
choices: You receive 100 shares for free
You must buy 100 shares at $100, an $8 per share paper loss offset by the premium received
Nothing; only calls can be exercised
You sell 100 shares at $100
questions.explain: Assignment on a short put means buying the shares at the strike. You pay $100 for stock worth $92; the premium you collected reduces the net loss.

questions.q: Which of these is a complete, testable entry rule?
choices: Buy strong stocks on dips
Buy when the close crosses above the 20-day SMA while the 50-day SMA is rising
Buy when it feels right
Buy whatever is trending on social media
questions.explain: A rule is testable when a computer could check it on every bar. "Strong", "dip" and "feels right" are not defined; the SMA rule is.

questions.q: A backtest shows +18% over a period in which buy-and-hold on the same stock returned +25%. The strategy:
choices: Beat the market because 18% is positive
Underperformed its benchmark; it added costs and effort for less return
Cannot be evaluated without the Sharpe ratio
Is overfit
questions.explain: Buy-and-hold is the free alternative. A strategy must beat it, or at least match it with much lower drawdown, to justify existing. Positive is not the same as good.

questions.q: Equity grows from $100,000 to $150,000 over three years. The CAGR is about:
questions.explain: CAGR = (150,000 / 100,000)^(1/3) - 1 = 1.5^(0.333) - 1, about 14.5% per year. Dividing 50% by three years (16.7%) ignores compounding.

questions.q: A strategy was in a position for 200 of 500 bars and matched buy-and-hold's return. Its exposure is:
questions.explain: Exposure is time in the market: 200 / 500 = 40%. Matching the benchmark while exposed only 40% of the time means less risk for the same return, which is a genuine improvement.

questions.q: A backtest buys at the open of a bar whenever that same bar's close is above the SMA. The flaw is:
choices: Survivorship bias
Look-ahead bias: the close is not known at the open
Too few trades
Transaction costs
questions.explain: Using the close to decide a trade executed at the open uses information from the future. Rules must act on the next bar after the signal is known.

questions.q: SMA(23)/SMA(61) returned 300% in the test period while SMA(20)/SMA(60) and SMA(25)/SMA(65) each returned about 40%. The best interpretation is:
choices: 23/61 is the magic combination; trade it
The 300% result is overfit: the edge lives in the exact numbers, not the idea
All moving average systems are useless
The data must be wrong
questions.explain: A robust strategy shows a plateau of similar results across nearby parameters. A single sharp peak means the parameters fitted noise in that specific history and will not repeat.

questions.q: Testing a "buy the dip" rule only on today's S&P 500 members is an example of:
choices: Look-ahead bias
Survivorship bias: the companies the dips destroyed are missing
Walk-forward testing
Mean reversion
questions.explain: Today's index members are the survivors. Companies that fell and never recovered were removed, so a dip-buying test on the current list never meets its worst outcomes.

questions.q: You tuned a strategy on 2018-2022 data. The honest next step is to:
choices: Report the 2018-2022 results as expected performance
Run the unchanged rules on 2023-2024 data you have not used
Re-tune on 2023-2024 as well
Add more indicators until 2018-2022 improves further
questions.explain: Out-of-sample testing on data the rules never saw is the only way to tell an edge from a curve fit. Re-tuning on the new data would make it in-sample too.

questions.q: A strategy averages +0.30% per round trip before costs. Each round trip costs 0.10% in spread, 0.10% in slippage and 0.05% in commissions. Its net edge per trade is:
questions.explain: Costs total 0.25% per round trip, leaving 0.30% - 0.25% = +0.05%. A small gross edge can vanish entirely with slightly worse fills, which is why high-frequency strategies rarely survive costs.

questions.q: After a strategy backtests well, what should come before trading it with real money?
choices: Nothing; the backtest is proof
Forward testing it on the paper account or in Market Replay to check fills, slippage and your own discipline
Doubling the position size
Removing the stop-loss to improve returns
questions.explain: Forward testing reveals what backtests hide: slippage, missed fills, and whether you can actually follow the rules under pressure. Paper trading and replay are the bridge to live trading.

questions.q: A written strategy says "exit on a close below the 20-day SMA". Today the stock closed below it, but you are sure it will bounce. The disciplined action is:
choices: Hold, since conviction counts
Exit as the rule says, and note the urge to override in your journal
Move the exit rule to the 50-day SMA
Double the position at the lower price
questions.explain: A strategy only has a measurable edge if it is followed. Overriding it turns a tested system into discretionary trading. The journal is where the urge to deviate gets recorded and reviewed.

questions.q: Winning trades total $12,000 and losing trades total $8,000. The profit factor is:
questions.explain: Profit factor is gross profit divided by gross loss: 12,000 / 8,000 = 1.5. Above 1 means the strategy made money; much above 3 in a backtest is a warning sign of overfitting.

questions.q: In Market Replay with intrabar ticks turned on, in what order are the four prices of a bar revealed?
choices: Open, high, low, close, always in that order
Open, the extreme nearer the open, the other extreme, then the close
Close first, then the open, high and low
Low, high, open, close
questions.explain: Ticks approximate a bar's path as open, the extreme nearer the open, the other extreme, then the close. It is a model of the path, not a tape, which is why the lesson says stops protect you from most outcomes rather than all of them.

questions.q: During a replay drill you are tempted to open the dashboard on the same symbol to see how the year actually ended. What does the lesson say about this?
choices: It is fine, because the replay engine will detect it and adjust the scorecard
It is the first discipline the drills test: the engine hides the future from the chart, but only you can refuse to look it up
It is encouraged, because knowing the outcome makes the drill faster
It is only a problem when a real-data key is connected
questions.explain: The engine cannot stop you peeking. Replay only teaches anything if you refuse to look up what the stock did, do not search the real chart for that year, and do not rerun a session just to erase a loss.

questions.q: With ticks off, a market order placed after a signal fills at the last revealed price. Why does the lesson suggest stepping one more bar before entering?
choices: Because the engine rejects market orders on the signal bar
Because the last revealed price is that bar's close, which a real trader could only have traded at the next open
Because indicators are only updated every second bar
Because stop orders are cheaper after one extra bar
questions.explain: A real trader sees the close and can act at the next open. Stepping one bar after the signal and then entering at the market gives you the fill a live trader would actually have had, instead of pretending you bought a price you could not have seen.

questions.q: A "Ride the trend" session ends up 35% with eleven round trips and no shorts. According to the drill criteria, does it pass?
choices: Yes, because the return is well above the capture target
No, because the drill allows at most three round trips: churning fails it even when it makes money
Yes, as long as the drawdown stayed under 25%
No, because trend drills require at least one short
questions.explain: The ride-the-trend criteria are strict about activity: three round trips or fewer, no shorts, and at least 20% of the move captured. The trade count exists to force you to size the stop so that normal pullbacks do not take you out.

questions.q: In the range-trading drill RSI(14) is falling towards 30 and price is approaching the range's support. Which action matches the lesson?
choices: Buy at the market immediately so you do not miss the bounce
Place a buy limit at or just above support and let the market come to your price, or accept that there was no trade
Short the stock, because falling RSI confirms the downtrend
Wait for RSI to reach 70 before buying
questions.explain: Reversal trades are won at the entry: the edge is only a few percent per trade and chasing with a market order gives half of it away. Limit orders at support, with a resting stop a little under the range low, are the whole lesson of that drill.

questions.q: In the 1% rule drill a $200 stock has a stop $6 below your entry in a calm month and $16 below it in a volatile month. With $100,000 of equity, how do the two position sizes compare?
choices: Identical: the 1% rule fixes the share count at 500
About 166 shares in the calm month versus 62 in the volatile month: the dollar risk stays the same while the size changes by roughly three times
62 shares in the calm month versus 166 in the volatile month, because volatility calls for more shares
The rule does not apply when the stop is more than $10 away
questions.explain: Risk budget is $1,000 either way. $1,000 / $6 = 166 shares (about $33,000); $1,000 / $16 = 62 shares (about $12,400). Position size is an output of the stop distance, never an input.

questions.q: A replay session loses money but you placed every stop as an order, took every signal and skipped nothing. What rating (1 to 5) does the lesson say the session deserves?
choices: A 1, because the account lost money
A 5, because the rating grades how well you followed the plan, not the profit
A 3, splitting the difference between process and result
No rating: losing sessions should not be journaled
questions.explain: The rating column grades rule-following regardless of outcome. A losing session where every rule was followed is a 5; a winning session where you abandoned the stop and got lucky is a 1 or 2. That column is the one that transfers to a live account.

questions.q: When a drill is repeated, why does the lesson say a run that only works because you remembered where the big moves were is a form of look-ahead bias?
choices: Because the engine replays different bars the second time
Because demo bars are deterministic, so knowledge of the first run leaks the future into the second run just as peeking at later data corrupts a backtest
Because the scorecard ignores repeated sessions
Because look-ahead bias only applies to indicators, not to traders
questions.explain: Demo bars are the same every time, so after one run you know the right-hand side of the chart. A repeat is only an honest experiment if the one changed rule would apply on any chart (stop distance, average length, size), not one that happens to fit these bars.

questions.q: Which of these is the lesson's test for whether a goal belongs in the trading plan?
choices: It must mention a dollar amount
A number in the journal export or on the Journal page's stats must be able to tell you whether you hit it
It must be achievable within one month
It must be more ambitious than beating the index
questions.explain: A goal you cannot measure from your journal is not a goal. For every line in the goals section, name the column or statistic that measures it; if none exists, rewrite the goal until one does.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the plan's outcome goal should be stated against an index ETF such as SPY?
choices: Because SPY has the lowest volatility of any instrument
Because the index fund is the yardstick: what you could have earned by simply buying it instead of trading
Because brokers require a benchmark before opening an account
Because the course certificate is only awarded for beating SPY
questions.explain: Module 1 introduced the index ETF as the yardstick. Beating a savings account while an index fund made 15% is not a success, which is why the backtest page prints buy-and-hold next to every result.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the sensible size of a daily-timeframe watchlist for a student trading after work?
choices: Two or three names, so nothing is missed
Roughly 15 to 30 names you actually know
At least 200 names, to maximise the number of signals
The whole S&P 500
questions.explain: Smaller and better known beats larger and anonymous. With 200 names the signals you take are the ones that happened to catch your eye, which is not a rule. Review the universe quarterly, not weekly.

questions.q: What is the course's default time stop for a daily swing setup, and why does a time stop exist at all?
choices: Two bars, because any trade that does not work immediately is wrong
Ten bars without progress, because capital sitting in a dead trade is unavailable for live signals and stale trades often turn into losses
Fifty bars, to give every trend time to develop
There is no default: time stops are discouraged
questions.explain: The exits section lists four exits: initial stop, target, time stop and trail. Ten bars is the common default for a daily swing time stop; its job is to free capital from trades going nowhere, which journals show tend to become losers.

questions.q: Your plan says risk per trade is 1% but a setup is in its first 30 paper trades. What risk does the lesson prescribe?
choices: 2%, to reach 30 trades faster
0.5%, half the normal risk, until the setup has passed its first 30 trades
Exactly 1%: the figure never changes
0%, because new setups should only be backtested
questions.explain: The risk rules set 1% as the course default and 0.5% while a setup is in its first 30 paper trades. The same halving applies at the first drawdown threshold, and normal risk is restored only after a new equity high.

questions.q: Your backtest passes with $1 commission and 10 bps slippage but the edge disappears when costs are doubled to $2 and 20 bps. What does the lesson conclude?
choices: The rule is fine, because live costs will never be that high
The rule is cost-sensitive and belongs on a slower timeframe or not at all
The rule should be run with zero costs to see its true edge
The rule passes gate 1 as long as the in-sample profit factor is above 1.3
questions.explain: The doubled-costs run is one of gate 1's four checks (in-sample, out-of-sample, sensitivity, costs doubled). An edge that vanishes with higher costs is too thin to trade on that timeframe.

questions.q: Over 30 trades with a 50% win rate, roughly what is the 95% range of the measured win rate, and what does that imply?
choices: 45% to 55%, so 30 trades is enough to confirm an edge
About 32% to 68%, so 30 trades cannot distinguish a slight edge from luck; its main proof is that you can follow written rules for months
0% to 100%, so paper trading is pointless
Exactly 50%, because the paper engine removes randomness
questions.explain: The standard error of a 50% win rate over 30 trades is about 9 percentage points, giving a 95% range of roughly 32% to 68%. Thirty trades mostly proves adherence and catches gross problems the backtest hid.

questions.q: Your monthly journal metrics show an average loss of 1.6R. What does the lesson say that indicates?
choices: Winners are too small relative to the stop
Stops are being moved further away or hit by gaps; look at the individual losing trades
Risk per trade should be raised to compensate
The benchmark is outperforming
questions.explain: Average loss in R should be close to 1.0 or below. Above about 1.2 means the planned 1R loss is being exceeded, which happens when stops are moved or when gaps blow through them.

questions.q: Under the plan's review cadence, which review is allowed to change a trading rule?
choices: The daily review, as soon as a rule fails
The weekly review, if the week was a losing one
The quarterly review, at most one change at a time, with the evidence written down and gate 1 rerun before adopting it
Any review, as long as the change is small
questions.explain: Daily and weekly reviews change nothing in the rules (weekly allows one behavioural commitment). Monthly may adjust risk per trade and the universe. Only the quarterly review changes rules, one at a time, with evidence, and re-runs the backtest gate first.

questions.q: According to the scaling rule in section 12 of the plan, when may you move from live trading at half risk to full risk?
choices: As soon as gate 3 passes
After thirty more trades with adherence above 90% and expectancy at or above zero
After one profitable month
When the maximum drawdown reaches the plan's limit
questions.explain: Scaling is a rule, not a feeling: live at half risk only after gate 3 passes; full risk only after thirty more trades with adherence above 90% and expectancy at or above zero; back to half risk at any drawdown threshold.
